Latest Update: PRC’s Angel Booth on the state of reverse title and settlement operations

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s no substitute for experience, as the time-worn cliché goes, and Angel Booth of Premier Reverse Closings (PRC) has spent nearly a quarter century building her knowledge base across the intersection of reverse mortgages and title and settlement services.
  • “I’ve been doing this going on 24 years,” Booth told HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily during the recent National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA)’s Annual Meeting & Expo in San Antonio.
  • In this edition of RMD’s Monday Morning Q&A, Booth offers her thoughts on the state of reverse mortgage business amid higher interest rates and slower home sales, the key risk assessments that her organization provides to lenders and servicers, and the need to train the next generation of title and settlement professionals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s no substitute for experience, as the time-worn cliché goes, and Angel Booth of Premier Reverse Closings (PRC) has spent nearly a quarter century building her knowledge base across the intersection of reverse mortgages and title and settlement services.

“I’ve been doing this going on 24 years,” Booth told HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily during the recent National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA)’s Annual Meeting & Expo in San Antonio. “I’ve done every role you can think of in an operation, from filing paperwork to answering phones, running a desk, managing an office and now being in sales. I recently got a promotion into a role where I’m the vice president of operations and the national sales manager as well. It’s basically things I’ve been doing already.”.

In this edition of RMD’s Monday Morning Q&A, Booth offers her thoughts on the state of reverse mortgage business amid higher interest rates and slower home sales, the key risk assessments that her organization provides to lenders and servicers, and the need to train the next generation of title and settlement professionals.

Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Pierson: Business is slow across the mortgage industry and that’s evident in Home Equity Conversion Mortgage numbers. As title and settlement providers, you’re also reliant on closing more loans. Has it been discouraging to see HECM business running so low or has much of that shifted over to proprietary products?

Booth: Well, it’s two parts, because we are a national division, but we primarily do reverse mortgages. We don’t have a shop with our title and settlement licenses where we do forward business with any regularity. We’re part of a bigger conglomerate and we have sister companies where, if it’s a forward home purchase, we’ll ask one of our sister companies to take that on.

As far as the numbers go, it’s a little slower than normal. Maybe the past three years have been not so great for us on the reverse side as well, but it’s not as slow as it is for some of our sister companies on the forward side. There’s some concern just because it’s that time of the year where we ebb and flow. But we are every bit as busy closing loans. We have difficult files and they’re pushing through those every day.

Pierson: Benutech recently published a report about mismatches between reverse mortgage servicing records and title records. How do you avoid these situations? Do servicers need to be more proactive or have good business partners to catch these errors?

Booth: With a reverse mortgage, not all the time, but many times, it could be the last loan [on the property]. So whether there’s a trust, whether a power of attorney was used, whatever that vesting looks like, that would have all been approved when that person got the loan. If something’s going to change, that borrower should be consulting or going to their servicer before they’re making any changes. But that doesn’t happen.

Industry observers note that we’ll be midway through a transaction. We put a date down on a file to get ready for closing and find that the borrower has recorded another deed or did something they weren’t supposed to do. If they’re early on in the process, maybe they’re changing their vesting and they’re taking it out of the trust or they’re putting it in a trust. They’ve added someone to the title, not realizing that, no, you can’t do that.

We run into problems with that when we’re trying to clear a file, because now there’s deceased parties, or this borrower and their family member don’t talk anymore, they’re not going to sign off, or they want money to sign off. I think it’s just a matter of borrowers sometimes doing their own thing. They might get misguided information from an attorney — not that their attorney is trying to intentionally give them the wrong information, but they’re not looking at it through a title lens.

I’m not going to bash title companies; there’s a reality there. Some companies have more resources and have more of a footprint in the space. Some of them are using AI tools — they’re not actually using as many humans to do the job. Yes, AI is helpful and it’s effective, but you still need a person to make sure these records are being checked.

According to recent reports, we’ve caught quite a few things within our searches. We’re in 45 states, so sometimes we’re dealing with an abstract, or sometimes we’re dealing with our in-house title department, and there’s discrepancies we have to address. Our lenders don’t always like it. They’re like, “Why are we dealing this from 20 years ago?” We’re like, “There’s something missing and we’re not finding it. We need more information to lock that in.” We are a very conservative title company, so we catch those things and we address them.

Sources indicate that there are some title companies who will write past that. And that’s how you end up down the line where there’s a foreclosure, the heirs are trying to take the property back or refinance it, and there are clouds because the title manufacturer may have taken something on as a risk that the lenders love in the moment. But they don’t love it when they’re trying to get that property off their books and they can’t because there’s some type of a vesting issue or ownership issue that they can’t get past, outside of taking it to court.

Pierson: Panelists who spoke at NRMLA Annual indicated lingering reputational concerns with the reverse mortgage product. Past celebrity marketing campaigns were referenced as something to possibly try again. From your perspective, what needs to be done to put the right messaging out there?

Booth: The biggest conversations I’ve been having are around information. It might be the loan officer who’s not fully trained and doesn’t fully understand the product to sell it, or it’s someone who fully understands the product and can sell it, but they don’t have an audience to connect with and get that message to.

I won’t say we should dumb it down, but we should break down that information so people can absorb it, retain it and actually use it moving forward. We just have to continue to inform people and make sure they know the right things — and correct them when it’s the wrong thing.

It has been revealed that I don’t know if the reputation will ever go away. But I do know what won’t make it go away is if people are not doing these loans for the right reasons, and we have more borrowers that maybe have a bad experience — even if it’s nowhere near what happened in the late 1990s, early 2000s. I think that should be the goal: The lender, the broker, the title firm, even the notary should be trying to make sure that the reverse mortgage experience is a good one.

It has been revealed that having the Reverse Mastermind Summit being a presence and growing is great. I think that people outside of NRMLA are doing things, taking reverse knowledge to other conventions, boards and groups to just get those conversations going. Start talking about reverse mortgages in a positive light. Educate people who are curious. I just did a conference with the National Association of Default Professionals. I’d never heard of it before. It’s REO. They’re interested in finding more information on reverse mortgages: “How can we figure out what to do when we run into a property where someone has passed away?”.

Industry observers note that pierson: Let’s discuss reverse for purchase deals, which were a focus at NRMLA Annual. They could be poised to take off as more real estate agents gain awareness. From a title and settlement services perspective, are you able to do them on the timelines that lenders want?

According to recent reports, booth: With lenders, I say we are family. They’re like our cousins and we don’t always use the same lingo within the family. A lot of what lenders are saying when they use that 10- to 15-day closing number, they’re not factoring in the onset — the contract being done and everything that goes into people looking and buying. That’s not a 10- to 15-day thing. But once a file is actually clear to close, that time frame is absolutely attainable.

Recent findings suggest that we actually don’t take on many purchase transactions, again because we focus primarily on the first-mortgage refinance. We do proprietary loans as well, but those sister companies where we have people who are doing purchases regularly, we would much rather them take on those deals than us do something, because we don’t ever want to cause an issue. Maybe there’s a upcoming form or a new procedure that we’re not privy to because we don’t do them every day. I do think there’s always going to be a reasonable time to get those done as long as everyone’s involved, everyone’s informed, everyone’s communicating.

Pierson: Training and education are ongoing topics of interest across housing. Most companies have employees who are aging out and need to identify fresh blood to replace them. What is the title and settlement industry doing on this front?

Industry observers note that booth: A lot of it comes from who you know. On the title and settlement positions that we put out there, it’s kind of like, ‘Hey, I don’t necessarily know what this thing is, but I’m going to try it.’ And we gauge whether you’re going to pick up this or you’re not, because it’s hard to explain.

People can go to school to get a real estate license. You can go get trained to be a Realtor or a loan originator. But there’s really no training for title and settlement work, so you’re looking at skill sets. You’re looking at character. You’re looking at people who are able to have retention and you just give them a try. That’s what happened to me — someone took a chance on me.

In a recent development, in the role I’m in now, and looking toward the future, we’re looking at college campuses, college fairs, or finding interns at the high school level. Not every kid is going to college, and if you can help them out while they’re figuring it out, they might pick up something that can turn into a career for them. We’re thinking about younger blood, younger people, who maybe aren’t tainted and haven’t learned things the wrong way. We can get them early before they’ve got all these different ideas and teach them the right way, at least in our operation.

We do cross-training quite a bit in our operation, to make sure everyone is learning the pieces of the puzzle. Sometimes you might have a group or a team who only do this one thing, and they know nothing about this other part and how it comes together. We’re trying to help people understand how the bigger process works. But that takes time.

BYD and Geely approached FIA about a 12th F1 team, says Ben Sulayem

💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD and Geely have both approached the FIA about entering Formula 1, the sport’s governing body confirmed.
  • But there’s no open process for a 12th team, and neither company has a deal.
  • “One of them was BYD and another was Geely,” Ben Sulayem stated of the manufacturers that have reached out about joining the grid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD and Geely have both approached the FIA about entering Formula 1, the sport’s governing body confirmed. FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem named the two Chinese automakers while speaking at the New Economy Forum in Madrid, as first reported by Grande Prêmio.

But there’s no open process for a 12th team, and neither company has a deal. The FIA is also pushing F1 toward the kind of engine an EV maker has the least reason to build.

“One of them was BYD and another was Geely,” Ben Sulayem stated of the manufacturers that have reached out about joining the grid.

Sources indicate that he said he suggested that BYD buy an existing team instead of starting a newly introduced one. BYD wasn’t interested in that route. It wants its own team, so Ben Sulayem told the company to come back with a “serious proposal” that indicates the project can work.

In a recent development, he also made it clear that Chinese manufacturers won’t get special treatment. Any bid would go through the same process as other prospective entrants, and the rules won’t be rewritten to suit them. Right now, there’s no expansion process at all: the FIA isn’t actively looking for a 12th team.

Still, Ben Sulayem repeated that he’d like F1’s next newcomer to come from China, pointing to the country’s EV technology and the Chinese Grand Prix in Shanghai.

Sources indicate that this isn’t new for BYD. Back in March, we reported that BYD was exploring a Formula 1 entry, either by buying a team or building one from scratch.

According to recent reports, in April, executive vice president Stella Li said BYD had met F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali in Shanghai and that an entry was “something we’re discussing.” By July, the tone had cooled. Li said “the dream is always there, but we don’t have a concrete agenda,” and special advisor Alfredo Altavilla set a clear condition: “We will never participate in Formula 1 just to put a sticker on the side of a car.”.

Altavilla mentioned BYD would only consider F1 to the extent its technology can serve the sport.

Geely is the upcoming name here. The group sold 3.02 million vehicles last year and owns Volvo, Polestar, and Lotus, a brand with decades of F1 history. It’s also heading into Canada next year as Chinese automakers push hard into new markets.

It has been revealed that the last newcomer, Cadillac, took a long road. The FIA opened an expression-of-interest process in 2023, and GM’s team only joined the grid as the 11th team this season, running Ferrari power until its own power unit arrives. Audi got in the other way, by taking over Sauber.

Here’s where it gets awkward for an EV maker. The 2026 F1 power units split output roughly 50/50 between the combustion engine and electric power, with the MGU-K jumping to 350 kW.

According to recent reports, the FIA is already walking that back. In June, it agreed to shift the split to 60-40 in favor of combustion for 2027 and 2028. And Ben Sulayem has been pushing for V8 engines running on sustainable fuel with “minor electrification” for the next rules cycle, starting in 2031 at the latest, possibly 2030. Domenicali notes F1 should have a package ready to discuss by the end of this year.

So the FIA president wants a Chinese EV maker on the grid, while pushing a rulebook that makes their main strength less relevant.

We like the idea of BYD or Geely in F1. Chinese automakers have the money and the engineers, and they badly need brand prestige outside China. BYD in particular has been on a performance push with Yangwang, and F1 would be the loudest possible way to tell Europe it’s not just a cheap car brand.

Industry observers note that they look for visibility/recognition on the world stage, regardless EVs. And in some (primitive) markets they market themselves as hybrids automakers, not as EV automakers.

They will make a hybrid power unit (which they already make anyway) to comply with the backward F1 regulations.

But Ben Sulayem’s comments don’t move things much. There’s no entry process, BYD has already turned down his main suggestion, and Geely’s interest is a name dropped at a conference, not a bid.

A Chinese would likely be good for F1 as well. Motorsports are on the rise in China, and that would be the cherry on top in helping popularize the sport in the world’s largest market.

The bigger issue is the engine. Altavilla was clear that BYD isn’t interested in slapping a logo on a car. It wants F1 to showcase its technology, and BYD’s technology is batteries and electric drive. The FIA’s V8 push goes the other way. It’s hard to sell an EV giant on a sport that’s reducing the electric part of the powertrain.

#144807. Industry News: More closings can mean less profit; the velocity illusion for builders

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1952 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: More closings can mean less profit; the velocity illusion for builders

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, one number goes missing from most corporate growth stories.
  • Homebuilding executives love closings.
  • According to recent reports, A company can sell more homes, acquire more land, and consume more capital while earning less on every additional closing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one number goes missing from most corporate growth stories. Not revenue. Not market share. Not units sold. The missing metric? What does the next unit actually earn?

Homebuilding executives love closings. Wall Street loves growth. Boards celebrate scale. But a closing is not a profit, revenue is not a return, and becoming the fifth-largest builder doesn’t necessarily make you the fifth-best business.

According to recent reports, A company can sell more homes, acquire more land, and consume more capital while earning less on every additional closing. Management calls it momentum. Shareholders may eventually discover it was deterioration.

That’s the velocity illusion: movement mistaken for progress.

It has been revealed that scale multiplies whatever you already are. If the underlying business creates economic value, growth can amplify it. If the underlying business destroys value, growth can accelerate the destruction.

Three companies learned that lesson the expensive way: MoviePass, Katerra, and Zillow Offers. Two operated directly in housing. Together, they turned billions of dollars of investor capital into volume that never earned its keep. All three offer a warning for homebuilders.

The more customers used the product, the more money the tech giant lost. Over the first nine months of 2018, Helios and Matheson reported $205.0 million in revenue and $424.4 million in cost of revenue – about $2.07 spent for every $1 collected, before any overhead. The gross loss was $219.4 million.

To fund the gap, the tech giant kept issuing stock. Its share count rose more than 3,000% in a year. In July 2018, it executed a 1-for-250 reverse split to stay listed on Nasdaq. By the following year, the stock had lost more than 99.99% of its value from its late-2017 peak.

The tech giant expected to report a 2018 net loss attributable to shareholders of approximately $266.8 million. Revenue fell from $234 million in 2018 to $24 million in 2019. In January 2020, MoviePass and its parent filed for Chapter 7 liquidation.

MoviePass had demonstrated demand, but not profitable demand. Customers weren’t necessarily expressing loyalty to a differentiated experience. They were accepting a subsidy.

According to recent reports, moviePass wasn’t scaling a viable subscription model. It was scaling a subsidy.

Sources indicate that katerra set out to industrialize construction by integrating design, engineering, procurement, manufacturing, logistics and installation. The theory was seductive: control the whole process, remove fragmentation, and win through scale.

It raised close to $3 billion in equity, more than $2 billion of it from SoftBank, and was valued at more than $4 billion.

In December 2019, CEO Michael Marks said annual revenue had doubled to roughly $1.7 billion and headcount had grown from 6,000 to 8,000. That figure was management’s public description, not an audited revenue figure. The same week, Katerra confirmed it was closing a 250,000-square-foot factory in Phoenix and laying off 200 workers.

In a recent development, bankruptcy filings later showed $2.78 billion in losses across 2018, 2019, and 2020. Measured against the equity raised, Katerra lost roughly 93 cents of every dollar investors put in. Its own chief transformation officer described projects with “significant cost overruns, resulting in massive, ongoing losses.”.

In a recent development, in December 2020, SoftBank provided another $200 million rescue – $175 million in cash and $25 million in loan forgiveness. It wasn’t enough. Katerra filed for Chapter 11 in June 2021 with about 6,400 employees, estimating liabilities of $1 billion to $10 billion against assets of $500 million to $1 billion.

According to recent reports, projects won at guaranteed prices and steep discounts became economically destructive. Sophisticated manufacturing infrastructure could not compensate for weak project economics.

Industry observers note that A factory doesn’t produce economies of scale merely by existing. Average unit costs must actually decline enough to support the facilities, equipment, fixed payroll, logistics, and capital it requires.

Traditional field construction has inefficiencies, but subcontractor capacity can adjust when a local market slows. An expensive factory is less flexible. When its volume disappears, the overhead stays.

Katerra built the apparatus of national scale before proving that the next project would reliably earn money.

Three billion dollars in equity did not change that equation.

Zillow possessed extraordinary housing data: transaction histories, consumer traffic, pricing algorithms and national market intelligence. Zillow Offers attempted to translate those advantages into a large-scale homebuying and resale business.

Sources indicate that in Q3 2021, it purchased 9,680 homes but sold 3,032. It ended the quarter holding 9,790 homes, with another 8,172 under contract. Inventory accumulated faster than the business could renovate and sell it.

Zillow recorded a $304.4 million inventory write-down that quarter. Zillow Offers posted a negative gross profit of about $245 million – an average loss of $80,771 per home sold, nearly 21% of revenue. The figures reflect segment accounting, including write-downs on homes not yet sold, not a uniform cash loss on every completed sale.

In a recent development, that distinction is the point. Excluding those write-downs, Zillow’s average return on the homes it actually sold that quarter was still positive, about $9,183 before interest. The completed sales looked fine. The damage was sitting in the homes it had just bought.

For the full year, the Homes segment generated $6.0 billion in revenue and lost $881.5 million before taxes, on 15,436 homes sold. That’s roughly $57,000 lost for every home Zillow sold in 2021. Inventory write-downs totaled $407.9 million, and wind-down charges recognized in 2021 reached $491.2 million.

In a recent development, zillow shut the operation down and cut about 25% of its workforce, roughly 2,000 jobs. Its shares fell 25% the day after the announcement. By then, the firm’s market value had dropped $30.5 billion from its February 2021 peak.

In a recent development, the failure involved pricing errors, renovation capacity, inventory exposure and changing market conditions. But the central lesson is familiar to anyone who has underwritten land.

A national average cannot tell you everything about a particular house. The block, drainage, school line, street noise, lot orientation or odd floor strategy can change what a buyer will pay.

Industry observers note that data can inform local judgment. It cannot replace it.

Sources indicate that zillow could buy houses very promptly. That did not mean it could buy, improve, and resell each one at a profit.

Each organization could point to a growing number. None could show that the next unit made money.

Consider a hypothetical builder selling homes for $400,000 each. It expands into new markets, layers on management, standardizes products and chases closings. Volume rises, but incentives and complexity gradually consume the margins.

The manufacturer increases closings fivefold. Revenue rises from $400 million to $2 billion. Yet annual operating profit moves from $48 million to a $40 million loss.

Recent findings suggest that that calculation excludes the additional land, development, construction inventory, and financing required to support the growth. The manufacturer is bigger. Its economics are worse. The point is not that growth always reduces margins. Closings alone cannot reveal whether growth creates value.

An notable distinction exists between high fixed overhead and negative contribution margins.

It has been revealed that if an additional sale contributes profit before fixed overhead, increased volume may legitimately improve total earnings. But suppose the directly attributable costs are $405,000 for a house that sells for $400,000. Each incremental closing loses $5,000 before any excluded overhead.

In a recent development, one thousand closings destroy $5 million. Five thousand destroy $25 million. Ten thousand destroy $50 million.

Sources indicate that that isn’t a theoretical exercise. MoviePass spent about $2.07 to deliver each dollar of revenue. Zillow’s Homes segment lost roughly $57,000 for every home it sold in 2021 – more than 10 times the $5,000 example.

In homebuilding, timing amplifies the consequences. Capital is committed to land, entitlements, infrastructure, construction, interest and property taxes long before the closing proceeds arrive. A bad land assumption can be repeated across an entire community.

According to recent reports, A $5,000 mistake repeated across 10,000 homes is $50 million. Scale multiplies mistakes just as efficiently as savings.

And averages can conceal the marginal problem. A builder can report respectable historical margins while the last homes sold—those discounted to meet a quarterly target—generate almost nothing. Zillow’s completed sales showed a positive average return in the same quarter its newest inventory was written down by $304 million.

Imagine a national builder acquires a successful local operator. Corporate purchasing eliminates product variations and saves $2,000 per home. But the standardized offering is less attractive to local buyers, so sales teams add $10,000 in incentives to maintain velocity.

Recent findings suggest that purchasing reports success. Sales reports more closings. Corporate reports higher revenue. The underlying economics have deteriorated by $8,000 per home, before other effects. Across 5,000 homes, that’s $40 million.

This is illustrative, but the management trap is real. Departments optimize the numbers they own while no one is accountable for the total return on the capital invested.

The purchasing department may celebrate a saving while the field absorbs delays, rework and incentive costs. Those expenses don’t vanish; they are recorded somewhere else. Management celebrates what it can count while weakening what creates economic value.

Closings are an activity measure. The scoreboard should follow the economics. What did the marginal home earn after incentives, rate buydowns, construction costs, expected warranty obligations and rework? What return did the latest community produce on its invested capital? Did the division generate cash after funding its land and inventory needs? Did average cost per comparable home actually fall as volume increased?

Industry observers note that and how much demand would exist without the incentive? Discounting finished inventory can be a rational way to release trapped capital. But a temporary inventory decision is not the same as a business model that permanently depends on subsidies to sustain volume.

Recent findings suggest that one is capital management. The other is a warning.

The velocity illusion is most dangerous when growth comes through acquisition. A homebuilder that buys local operators is paying for distinct judgment, brands, and customer relationships. If it then places one acquired firm’s systems over the rest, it should be able to prove that those systems improve the businesses beneath them. A larger platform isn’t proof. Neither are awards, rankings, or a higher closing count.

The evidence is in the numbers most companies don’t publish: division-level profitability, return on invested capital, community-level land economics, and how much purchasing efficiency survives after incentives, carrying costs, lost product differentiation, and operating disruption.

And owners should ask what happened to the local talent and judgment they paid to acquire.

Difficult markets, interest rates, incentives, product mix, and geography all influence results. They can explain a bad year. They cannot, by themselves, prove an integration created value.

Recent findings suggest that if an operating philosophy is making strong local businesses less distinctive or less profitable, the owner should change the operating structure – not sacrifice the assets that justified the acquisitions. Patience is a virtue. Patience without financial accountability can become an extraordinarily expensive mistake.

Before celebrating another thousand homes, prove what the next one earns. Before entering another market, prove the existing markets generate acceptable returns. Before giving one acquired company authority over the rest, prove that its methods improve their economics rather than erase their advantages.

Recent findings suggest that the opportunity in American homebuilding was never merely to become larger. It is to combine product excellence with entrepreneurship, local land judgment and trusted brands. That opportunity is still available. But it requires evidence – not optimism—that the operating model works.

Scale is not a strategy. It’s an amplifier. If the unit creates value, scale can multiply the success. If the unit destroys value, scale industrializes the loss.

Newly introduced product debuts and partnerships this month highlight how real estate technology companies are using AI, payments innovation and listing integrations to streamline transactions and give agents more measurable value from their tools.

RealScout has turned on Zillow Preview listings inside its collaborative home search platform, giving agents and their buyers earlier visibility into homes before they become active on the MLS.

First declared in September, the integration is now live for RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 real estate professionals across the U.S., according to the company announcement.

It has been revealed that zillow Preview lets sellers market their homes on Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com before they go active on the MLS, while allowing agents to comply with local MLS rules. Participating brokerages can also choose to syndicate those Preview listings to RealScout, increasing exposure to buyers who are searching with their own agents.

Why it matters for housing professionals: As pocket listings, coming-soon inventory and off-MLS marketing continue to draw scrutiny from regulators and MLSs, structured preview programs and controlled distribution channels give listing brokers a way to build early demand while keeping agents and buyers inside a compliant workflow.

BrokerBot secured new capital, including a strategic investment from the California Association of Realtors (CAR) and follow-on funding from Grand Ventures and other investors, and released BrokerBot 2.0, its upgraded AI platform for brokerages and associations.

The announcement comes shortly after BrokerBot won the $15,000 grand prize at NAR’s Tech & Innovation Pitch Battle at NAR NXT.

Sources indicate that brokerBot 2.0 positions itself as an “AI brain” for a brokerage or association, connecting multiple large language models to the organization’s documents, systems and communication channels. The company says the platform is SOC 2 compliant and E&O insured and that no model is trained on a client’s proprietary data.

CAR President Mark Peterson stated the association’s investment is intended to help ensure that AI tools for Realtors are “practical, secure and focused on delivering greater value to their clients.”.

According to recent reports, why it matters for housing professionals: As brokerages experiment with AI across marketing, transaction coordination and compliance, questions about data security and governance are becoming central to vendor selection. Backing from a large state association and an emphasis on SOC 2 controls could influence how firms evaluate AI platforms in 2027 budget cycles.

Zillow rolled out four newly introduced tools designed to answer what it calls the four core questions of moving: how much a buyer can afford, where to live, which home to choose and which agent to hire.

The tools, available across Zillow’s web and mobile apps depending on the feature, include:.

Zillow senior vice president of Product Cynthia Taylor mentioned the tools are aimed at putting “clear information” in front of consumers at each stage of the process.

According to recent reports, why it matters for housing professionals: More granular affordability, neighborhood and agent-matching tools on consumer platforms can shape lead quality and expectations before buyers ever talk to a lender or agent. Understanding how these features work can help professionals respond to better-informed — and sometimes more opinionated — clients.

Lofty released what it calls the industry’s first AI index for real estate, a benchmark intended to quantify how many tasks and hours its AI tools are saving agents across the country.

Recent findings suggest that according to the manufacturer’s November announcement, Lofty AI completed 1.13 million tasks in October 2026, saving real estate agents an estimated 131,248 hours by handling follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates. The Lofty AI Index breaks down results by task type, product, team or brokerage size and geography. More detail is available at the company’s website.

The launch comes as 81% of agents cite “saving time” as the primary reason for adopting fresh technology, according to NAR’s 2026 Realtors Technology Report, but many still struggle to measure impact.

Why it matters for housing professionals: Brokerages and teams under margin pressure are looking for hard numbers on productivity gains from AI and automation. If widely adopted, indices like Lofty’s could influence tech stack decisions, staffing models and how vendors are held accountable for ROI.

In a recent development, constellation Data Labs confirmed an expanded strategic partnership with Canva to support the underlying real estate data infrastructure for Canva’s enterprise real estate offering in the U.S. and Canada.

The collaboration is designed to remove the friction of licensing and normalizing MLS data so brokerages and agents can create compliant, on-brand marketing materials inside Canva using live listing feeds.

Constellation Data Labs will manage the data pipeline, MLS licensing workflow and compliance monitoring on behalf of Canva and its real estate clients. Once a brokerage is onboarded, agents can access their listing data directly within Canva to build dynamic marketing assets more swiftly.

In a recent development, why it matters for housing professionals: As listing marketing becomes more visual and omnichannel, agents need faster ways to turn accurate listing data into compliant campaigns. Offloading MLS data complexity to a specialist while using a familiar design platform could reduce turnaround times for print, social and digital assets.

Earnnest rolled out its Cash to Close solution nationwide, extending its digital payments platform beyond earnest money deposits to help homebuyers fund closings electronically instead of using wires or cashier’s checks.

Industry observers note that the firm began piloting Cash to Close with select settlement companies in July and says it has successfully supported transactions across five states. With the national launch, settlement companies across the country can now use the tool.

Earnnest’s expansion builds on its experience processing more than 1 million escrow payments without a single instance of fraud or a chargeback against an escrow holder, according to the announcement.

Why it matters for housing professionals: Wire fraud remains one of the biggest operational risks in residential real estate. Moving more closing funds into controlled digital workflows could change how brokerages, title companies and buyers handle payments, insurance requirements and consumer education at the end of the transaction.

Real Geeks unveiled AI Connect, a newly introduced feature that lets real estate agents use popular AI tools to redesign and optimize their IDX websites using natural language instructions.

The Dallas-based organization indicates AI Connect is a first-of-its-kind capability in the real estate IDX website space. Agents can work with tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok to create or update neighborhood pages, adjust site design, generate SEO-focused content and tailor pages for emerging AI search experiences — all through conversational prompts.

The goal is to help agents compete more effectively for leads in both traditional search engines and AI-powered search interfaces without needing deep technical or design skills.

Why it matters for housing professionals: As search behavior shifts toward AI assistants and vertical search tools, IDX sites that can quickly ship structured, localized content may have an advantage in visibility and lead capture. Features that turn AI prompts into site changes could influence how teams manage their web presence and content strategy.

Inform, a deep-tech spatial AI tech giant, rolled out today with technology that turns ordinary video of a property into a trusted 3D building record. Every year, millions of U.S. properties are measured, photographed and described by hand, often more than once, by appraisers, inspectors and insurance adjusters who each start from scratch. Instead, from one video, Inform rebuilds a building in 3D, works out its rooms, measurements and features, and keeps a record of exactly what the camera saw, so every fact about a property can be traced back to evidence.

It has been revealed that new EV prices edged up in October, but buyers still paid less than they did a year ago. The average transaction price for a new EV in the US was $56,220, up 1% from September and down 2.7% from October 2025, according to Kelley Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand.

Across all newly introduced vehicles, the average hit a record $51,109, up 1.3% from September and 2.1% year over year, even as prices rose more slowly than they typically do in October.

According to recent reports, EV incentives barely budged from September’s revised 11.2% of the average transaction price to 11.3% in October. That’s up from 10.3% a year earlier and well above October’s industrywide average of 6.8%.

In a recent development, tesla’s average selling price fell from September to $54,194, but it was still up 1.2% year over year. The Cybertruck helped push that average higher. Cox Automotive estimates Tesla sold 1,914 Cybertrucks in October, its best month in more than a year, at an average price of $92,380.

The sad thing is that there likely is a market for an affordable electric pickup truck in the U.S. to compete with Ford’s F150 and others. The Ford Fathom may be the best fit for that market, now.

In a recent development, that sales bump comes as Tesla prepares to end Cybertruck production at its Austin factory in mid-2027. Elon Musk remarked Tesla will dismantle the assembly line around June or July to make room for more Cybercab robotaxis.

NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.
  • According to recent reports, pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005.
  • It has been revealed that pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

According to recent reports, pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents mentioned.

It has been revealed that pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint mentioned he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

It has been revealed that white also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton mentioned it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”.

Sources indicate that pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also noted the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

According to recent reports, “NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

In a recent development, pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears stated the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

It has been revealed that “John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” mentioned David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Recent findings suggest that pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.

#144796. Real estate reputation is built through consistency and culture

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (776 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Real estate reputation is built through consistency and culture

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every brokerage can rank its agents by volume.
  • Recent findings suggest that sales volume and record-breaking transactions are meaningful measures of success.
  • We often talk about reputation as something an individual agent builds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every brokerage can rank its agents by volume. Far fewer can say what clients will remember about working with them five years later.

Recent findings suggest that sales volume and record-breaking transactions are meaningful measures of success. But after more than two decades in real estate, I’ve learned that they capture only the result, not the experience behind it. They don’t tell us whether an agent gave difficult advice at the right moment, brought the right people together or earned the kind of trust that leads to the next relationship.

We often talk about reputation as something an individual agent builds. In reality, it’s something an entire team has to deliver.

In luxury real estate, exceptional service is sometimes mistaken for extravagant gestures. More often, it comes down to something quieter: preparation, discretion, good judgment and following through on commitments.

Consistency doesn’t mean giving every client an identical experience. It means maintaining the same standards while understanding what matters to each person. One seller may want absolute privacy; another may expect detailed updates after every showing.

In New York City, where clients have many options and high expectations, candor matters just as much as polish. Sometimes the best service is telling a seller their home needs to be priced correctly from day one, rather than offering an appealing number that won’t stand up to the market.

Recent findings suggest that that conversation won’t appear in a production ranking. But it may be the reason the client calls again.

It has been revealed that an agent leads the relationship, but the client encounters the work of many people. Photography, staging, marketing, operations and strategic partnerships all shape the experience and ultimately an agent’s reputation.

As a leader, I believe one of our most vital responsibilities is creating an environment where agents have the resources, relationships and collaborative support to build exceptional businesses. The strongest agents aren’t operating in isolation. They’re surrounded by people who share their commitment to exceptional service.

Our recent relaunch of The Elysia at 200 East 59th Street is one example. Working alongside agents Michael Biryla and John Antretter and our partners at rennie, The Agency’s Latest York marketing and creative teams helped reintroduce the condominium with a refreshed identity and cohesive strategy.

In a recent development, from the property’s positioning and creative materials to its September relaunch event, each element reflected a shared vision. The result demonstrated how different areas of expertise can come together to create a cohesive client experience.

That’s the distinction between generating attention and earning confidence. When agents have a team working toward a common goal, they’re better equipped to deliver the thoughtful service that strengthens relationships over time.

It’s one thing to deliver a memorable experience once. It’s another to maintain that standard as a brokerage grows. A brand isn’t built by placing the same logo in more markets, nor is success defined solely by adding agents or offices. Meaningful growth comes from building a culture where people feel supported, collaboration is encouraged and the client experience remains exceptional regardless of location.

It has been revealed that throughout my career, I’ve learned that culture isn’t established through messaging alone. It’s reflected in how teams communicate, share knowledge and support one another. That means recognizing the marketers, operations professionals and specialists whose contributions strengthen agents’ businesses. Local expertise and individual character remain essential, but the same standards of professionalism, discretion and care should be reflected throughout the organization.

Reputation is rarely defined by a single transaction. It’s built through years of consistent decisions, meaningful relationships and sound guidance when clients need it most. In challenging markets, when buyers are selective and sellers face difficult decisions, clients rely on advisors who communicate honestly and guide them through uncertainty. Having difficult conversations, adjusting strategies and prioritizing clients’ long-term interests are what ultimately build lasting trust.

As leaders, our responsibility is to create a culture that reinforces those values and gives agents the support to uphold them. Production should be celebrated, but we should also recognize the repeat clients, referrals, collaboration and sound judgment that make it sustainable. The question isn’t simply who had the biggest year. It’s who has built an experience, and a team, that people will trust again.

That’s the kind of success that lasts.

A gain of about 0.5% in SHIB's price, with TAO's price unchanged, would be enough for the meme coin to take Bittensor's place in the ranking.

Sources indicate that TAO is the token of the Bittensor AI network, and Digital Currency Group (DCG) founder Barry Silbert has been one of its most vocal backers. Silbert also runs Yuma, a DCG company that builds on Bittensor.

In a recent development, at Fortune's Brainstorm Tech conference in September 2025, Silbert remarked that Bittensor was the thing he had gotten most excited about since Bitcoin. "I want to open up the development and the access to AI, and Bittensor is enabling that," he said at the time. Silbert also said that Bittensor is building a "world wide web of intelligence.".

In a recent development, on Dec. 30, 2025, DCG's Grayscale filed with the SEC to convert its Grayscale Bittensor Trust into a spot exchange-traded fund on NYSE Arca under the ticker GTAO. The filing came after Bittensor's first halving in mid-December 2025, and at the end of that month, TAO was trading at about $222. "We're pleased to take this early step as we continue to expand the tools available to investors," a Grayscale spokesperson said.

The gap between the two tokens closed because TAO fell. TAO was one of the market's strongest tokens this year. In April, the token was up 55% since January, and in October it rallied again and was up 43% for the year, according to TradingView data.

Recent findings suggest that the November correction erased those gains. On Nov. 20, TAO was trading 16.95% below its January level, and it lost 12.16% over the past week.

TAO had a 24-hour trading volume of $172.19 million on Nov. 20, and SHIB had $55.17 million, according to CoinMarketCap data. TAO has a maximum supply of 21 million tokens, the same as Bitcoin's, and SHIB has about 589 trillion tokens in circulation.

Lucid CEO admits it ‘did not even know where cars were’ and lost orders

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lucid (LCID) CEO Silvio Napoli admitted on the organization’s Q3 earnings call that, as recently as this summer, the automaker “did not even know where cars were.” Buyers placed orders, Lucid took up to two weeks to locate and deliver a car, and some of those buyers walked away.
  • That’s a rough admission from a company sitting on thousands of unsold vehicles.
  • Industry observers note that napoli made the comment when an analyst asked whether Lucid’s deliveries would go up or down in the fourth quarter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lucid (LCID) CEO Silvio Napoli admitted on the organization’s Q3 earnings call that, as recently as this summer, the automaker “did not even know where cars were.” Buyers placed orders, Lucid took up to two weeks to locate and deliver a car, and some of those buyers walked away.

That’s a rough admission from a company sitting on thousands of unsold vehicles. And it’s a problem Tesla ran into, and fixed, back in 2018 at more than ten times Lucid’s current volume.

Industry observers note that napoli made the comment when an analyst asked whether Lucid’s deliveries would go up or down in the fourth quarter. He remarked that at the start of Q3, the tech giant had orders where it “would take sometimes two weeks to deliver to the customer, and so we would lose the order.”.

He stated Lucid now has visibility on which cars are being built, where they’re shipped, where they’re stored, and when they can reach a customer. A new commercial team also now sells the cars it knows are available on the day a customer wants one.

Recent findings suggest that lucid built 3,228 more vehicles than it delivered in the first half of 2026, including 5,500 built but only 3,093 delivered in Q1. Its inventory hit $1.38 billion on the balance sheet at the end of June, which is why we reported earlier this year that Lucid had to adjust production after a bloated Q1 inventory.

So Lucid had thousands of cars on lots and in transit, and it was still losing buyers because it couldn’t match a car to an order fast enough.

According to recent reports, in Q3, Lucid cut production to 2,954 vehicles and delivered 3,806, down 7% year over year. Finished goods inventory fell by almost 15% during the quarter, according to new CFO Alexander De Bock. Inventory stood at $1.22 billion on September 30.

Tesla learned this lesson the hard way during the Model 3 ramp.

By Q3 2018, Tesla was making roughly 4,000 Model 3s per week. That’s more cars every week than Lucid delivers in a full quarter today. Deliveries tripled or quadrupled in some markets, and the bottleneck moved from the factory to the trucks.

Recent findings suggest that elon Musk tweeted in September 2018 that Tesla had “gone from production hell to delivery logistics hell.” A week later, he said Tesla was facing an “extreme shortage of car carrier trailers” and had started building its own car carriers to keep cars moving. Tesla also released door-to-door delivery and asked existing owners to help at delivery centers.

It didn’t stop there. In November 2018, with the federal tax credit about to be cut in half for Tesla buyers, Musk noted Tesla had bought trucking companies and locked in contracts with major haulers. Tesla moved cars east by truck instead of rail to cut weeks off transit times.

Tesla delivered 83,500 vehicles in Q3 2018, including 55,840 Model 3s, a record at the time.

When Model 3 reached Europe in February 2019, the first ship docked at Zeebrugge in Belgium and Tesla immediately had trouble processing the cars at the port.

According to recent reports, about a week after the first ship arrived, Tesla ended its contract with the tech giant preparing Model 3s at the port and took over the work itself. The target was 3,000 cars per week coming through one port.

It worked. By March 2019, Tesla delivered more than 5,300 Model 3s in Norway alone, making it the best-selling car in the country by a wide margin. A car that’s sitting at a port or on a lot doesn’t make anyone money. Tesla treated delivery speed as a sales tool, not a back-office job.

We later learned from Musk himself that this “logistic hell” was almost the nail in Tesla’s coffin. The CEO remarked that Tesla was at the brink of bankruptcy at the time.

I like to think people were relatively patient with Tesla's growing pains when Model 3 was ramping up in 2018, largely because there weren't many alternatives for a sporty, relatively affordable EV.

But it's 2026. Buyers have plenty of options now, and the patience that early EV adopters once had for these kinds of mistakes is long gone.

This is one of the most embarrassing admissions we’ve heard on an earnings call, and credit to Napoli for saying it out loud. Most executives would have blamed “demand” and moved on.

But it explains a lot. Lucid’s problem has never been the cars. The Air and Gravity are excellent products. The problem has been everything around them: service, software, and now we learn, basic inventory tracking. When you’re spending about $273,000 for every car you deliver, losing a buyer because you can’t find their car two weeks after they ordered is brutal.

Sources indicate that tesla solved this at 4,000 Model 3s a week while fighting for its own survival. Lucid is moving fewer than 300 cars a week. This isn’t a hard problem at that scale. It’s a discipline problem, and Napoli is right to call it that.

Breaking: Non-QM lending grows as buyers change financing strategies

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Homebuyers are increasingly willing to change their mortgage financing strategies to get into the housing market, helping drive growth in nonqualified mortgage (non-QM) lending according to latest research from Cotality.
  • Data presented during a Cotality webinar last week found that 69% of buyers initially cut lifestyle spending to make homeownership more affordable.
  • The findings point to growing demand for alternative mortgage products.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Homebuyers are increasingly willing to change their mortgage financing strategies to get into the housing market, helping drive growth in nonqualified mortgage (non-QM) lending according to latest research from Cotality.

Data presented during a Cotality webinar last week found that 69% of buyers initially cut lifestyle spending to make homeownership more affordable. But once these adjustments become insufficient, 65% turn to changing their financing options, according to the organization’s analysis of homebuyer behavior.

The findings point to growing demand for alternative mortgage products.

It has been revealed that “The economy and the way people earn income has changed,” remarked Selma Hepp, chief economist at Cotality. “Non-QM is becoming a permanent component of the mortgage market because the borrower base it serves is permanent.”.

Recent findings suggest that hepp pointed to the growing number of business owners, independent contractors, commission-based workers, real estate investors and households with multiple income sources. She cited approximately 11.9 million independent contractors, representing 7.4% of employment, and 9 million multiple-job holders, representing 5.5% of employed people.

In a recent development, many of these borrowers may have the financial resources to repay a mortgage but struggle to demonstrate their income through conventional underwriting. But Hepp cautioned that alternative underwriting should not be presented as a simple affordability solution. “What it can do is align underwriting more closely with what the borrower’s actual financial capacity is,” she mentioned.

Nonagency lending has expanded in recent years, driven primarily by non-QM loans, noted Patrick Kaiser, Cotality’s principal product manager in property intelligence.

Kaiser said non-QM lending was on pace to exceed 2025 volume by the end of 2026 and could grow again in 2027 if current trends continue. Loans for consumer borrowers remain the largest share of the market, but debt-service-coverage ratio (DSCR) loans for real estate investors are gaining ground.

Industry observers note that investor lending brings its own risks. Rising insurance premiums, property taxes and other operating costs can weaken rental-property cash flow, Hepp remarked. A softer labor market could also put pressure on borrowers with self-employment or variable income.

It has been revealed that but Holly Niemeier, a senior loan officer at NEXA Lending who works primarily with investors, told HousingWire that investor demand has kept her busy despite elevated borrowing costs. Her clients range from first-time investors to those with hundreds of properties, including some looking to acquire as many as 20 at a time.

Industry observers note that “People are having a hard time getting loans, and the investors now, the prices have dropped some, so I’m busier than I’ve ever been this month,” she noted. “The rates aren’t really affecting the investors. They’re still buying.”.

Niemeier said investors use different strategies depending on their available capital. Some buy properties with cash, renovate them and refinance, while others purchase turnkey rentals with existing tenants. Those who run low on capital may use hard money loans to acquire and renovate properties before refinancing into DSCR loans.

Virtually all of Niemeier’s investor business involves DSCR financing, either for individual properties or through portfolio loans. She also sees investors favoring lower-cost properties in urban markets such as St. Louis and Detroit, where smaller down payments can make it easier to expand a portfolio.

It has been revealed that “The investors don’t seem to flinch,” she mentioned. “They don’t change anything.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Chip Stocks News Commentary - Semiconductor stocks were out in front on Monday morning as buyers came back to the chip group after a week of heavy selling. The biggest spark came before the opening bell, when NVIDIA declared that its board had reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as President and Chief Executive Officer, and shares across the semiconductor supply chain moved higher with it, from AI processors and memory to the equipment that builds the chips. Active Companies in the semiconductor space with current developments include: NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA), Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MU), Intel Corporation (NASDAQ: INTC), Arm Holdings plc (NASDAQ: ARM), Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMAT).

The Founder Is Back at the Helm.

Sources indicate that NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA) announced on Monday that, effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The firm said the Board voted unanimously following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, and that it received input from senior levels of the United States government, on which basis the Board is confident that his reinstatement poses no national security risk. Huang had resigned on Nov. 12. NVIDIA also said its Board has formed a National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors, that it is recruiting a Chief Compliance Officer, and that Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, continues as Chief Financial Officer.

The business Huang returns to is growing fast. For its fiscal third quarter ended Oct. 25, 2026, NVIDIA reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 20% from the previous quarter and up 103% from a year ago, including Data Center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110% from a year ago. The tech giant mentioned its Vera Rubin NVL72 platform has shipped, and it expects fourth-quarter revenue of $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%, for a quarter that includes an additional week. NVIDIA noted that its outlook does not assume any Data Center compute revenue from China.

Memory Makers Ride the AI Build-Out.

In a recent development, micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MU) reported record fiscal fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 results, with fourth-quarter revenue of $54.23 billion, compared with $41.46 billion in the prior quarter and $11.32 billion in the same period a year earlier. Revenue for the full fiscal year, which ended Sept. 3, 2026, reached $133.19 billion, up from $37.38 billion in fiscal 2025.

Industry observers note that micron guided fiscal first-quarter 2027 revenue to $61.5 billion, plus or minus $1.5 billion, and CEO Sanjay Mehrotra stated the company expects an even stronger fiscal 2027. Investors will hear from the company again soon: Micron said its executives will take part in a fireside chat at the 30th Annual UBS Global Technology and AI Conference in Scottsdale, Arizona, on Tuesday, Dec. 1.

Processors From the Data Center to the Device.

Industry observers note that intel Corporation (NASDAQ: INTC) reported third-quarter 2026 results with revenue of $16.5 billion, up 21% year over year. Its Data Center and AI group posted revenue of $7.3 billion, up 78%, which Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner described as the manufacturer's strongest data center revenue growth in 15 years.

During the quarter, Intel unveiled prepares for a multiyear collaboration with Oracle intended to expand Intel Xeon-based computing on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. CEO Lip-Bu Tan noted the organization's immediate priority is to unlock additional supply to meet demand for its Xeon family, and Intel is forecasting fourth-quarter 2026 revenue of $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion.

Arm Holdings plc (NASDAQ: ARM) delivered a record second quarter for its fiscal year 2027, which ended Sept. 30, 2026, with total revenue of $1.44 billion, up 27% year over year and its fifth consecutive quarter of total revenue growth above 20%. Licensing and other revenue reached $773 million, up 50%, while royalty revenue was $670 million.

The reach of the Arm platform keeps widening. For the first time, Arm's partners reported more than 10 billion Arm-based chips shipped in a single quarter, an increase of 1.5 billion chips from a year earlier, on a platform used by more than 30 million developers. Arm also noted it is confident of achieving up to $2 billion in Arm AGI CPU revenue across fiscal years 2027 and 2028.

Recent findings suggest that applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMAT) reported record quarterly revenue for its fiscal fourth quarter of $10.41 billion, up 53% year over year, and record non-GAAP earnings per share of $4.16, up 92%. Annual revenue reached a record $34.45 billion, up 21%, and the manufacturer generated record quarterly cash from operations of $3.30 billion.

Industry observers note that applied Materials expects first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $11.1 billion, plus or minus $500 million, and non-GAAP earnings per share of $4.35, plus or minus $0.20. President and CEO Gary Dickerson said the company is on track to grow its Semiconductor Systems business more than 40% in calendar 2026.

It has been revealed that monday's move put the spotlight back on the numbers driving the industry. NVIDIA has its founder back in the top job and a $130.0 billion revenue outlook for its current quarter. In a recent development, the XRP price is struggling to take advantage of institutional credibility for the ledger. Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse has another explanation: Wall Street is pulling liquidity toward blockbuster IPOs.

According to recent reports, the XRP Ledger Foundation assessed the network against all ten principles in the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit. CertiK independently verified the network’s evidence under the Architecture and Resiliency principles.

Sources indicate that garlinghouse said investors have been moving money out of crypto, including XRP, to fund major listings. He expects the market to recover after Anthropic’s debut, just as it did following SpaceX’s IPO.

In a recent development, the GL1 toolkit gives financial institutions a common framework for assessing digital infrastructure. It has ten principles that cover governance, legal foundations, settlement finality, architecture, economic models, resilience, access, interoperability, privacy, and operations.

Sources indicate that this makes the assessment relevant to banks exploring tokenized markets. Institutions need to understand how networks handle operational risk, governance, and settlement before building financial products on them.

According to recent reports, the XRP Ledger Foundation has completed the attestation of the XRP Ledger against the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit. It is the first public, permissionless layer-1 blockchain to have the toolkit's Architecture and Resiliency principles independently… pic.twitter.com/wEKczeEdrF.

XRPL’s case is notable because it is public and permissionless. Traditional financial networks often operate behind controlled access. Public blockchains must show how risks are handled across distributed governance, protocol upgrades, and open participation.

The Foundation assessed XRPL against all ten principles. It also supplied supporting evidence for each control. CertiK then examined the Architecture and Resiliency sections, using code, configurations, logs, and test results.

CertiK noted it reviewed all 112 controls in the toolkit. Its technical verification focused on those suitable for independent assessment. The firm also verified Partior’s self-attestation under the same two principles.

Institutional adoption of digital assets depends on trust backed by independent verification and evidence.CertiK has completed independent technical verification of @XRPLF’s and Partior’s self-attestations under the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit,… pic.twitter.com/nQoEXjDHLh.

The XRPL Foundation called it the first such verification for a public, permissionless Layer 1. The milestone gives institutions a structured reference when evaluating networks for tokenized deposits, stablecoins, funds, and other assets.

According to recent reports, that is useful progress for XRPL’s institutional pitch. Risk and compliance teams can now examine evidence against familiar market-infrastructure standards. They have more than a blockchain’s own description of its capabilities.

In the interview, Garlinghouse addressed the gap between Ripple’s expansion and XRP price performance. He said the SpaceX IPO triggered a similar pullback as investors shifted liquidity out of crypto. He specifically named Bitcoin and XRP among the assets affected.

According to recent reports, investors moved capital from liquid crypto markets into the highly anticipated SpaceX listing, he mentioned. Garlinghouse sees the same pattern ahead of Anthropic’s debut.

Anthropic priced its shares at $83 and began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday. The offering covers 980 million shares, and the deal is expected to close Friday, November 20.

“What we saw after the SpaceX IPO was a rally in the crypto markets,” Garlinghouse said. “I think you’ll see that happen here as well.”.

He also expects digital assets to stop moving in lockstep. In his view, real utility and demand will increasingly separate stronger projects from speculative tokens. That puts the XRP price debate back on XRPL’s ability to attract activity.

Industry observers note that the presale has raised more than $33.2 million, with HYPER priced at just $0.0136. The November 26 deadline is now approaching, leaving less than a week before the scheduled presale close.

According to recent reports, XRPL’s latest institutional milestone demonstrates how infrastructure improvements can strengthen a blockchain’s appeal to financial players. Bitcoin Hyper is pursuing a different route, building an execution layer that could make Bitcoin more useful across payments and decentralized finance.

If Bitcoin Layer 2 adoption gains traction, projects delivering faster execution and financial applications could attract growing institutional attention. Bitcoin Hyper is positioning itself ahead of that opportunity, with its presale entering its final stretch.

Zcash leveraged bullish positions have come under pressure in the last 24 hours, with reported data showing a 1,483% liquidation imbalance in favor of long-position wipeouts.

Industry observers note that according to CoinGlass data, Zcash recorded more than $14 million ($14.07 million) in liquidations over 24 hours, with nearly 93% coming from long positions. Liquidated longs were $13.16 million against shorts of $917,620, a difference of 1,483%.

Long traders have taken most of the forced closures in this market, with Zcash being hit hard by the ongoing market sell-off. Significant long liquidations were seen for Zcash, accelerating its price decline as leveraged positions unwind, particularly with traders being heavily concentrated on the same side of the market.

At the time of writing, ZEC was down 14.53% in the last 24 hours, recording the heaviest losses in the top 20, while NEAR Protocol was down 13.03% in the same timeframe.

In a recent development, zcash is right now testing support at the 200-day MA ($809); a further drop would target $775 and then $700. A short-term price recovery for Zcash would see it aim for a return to four figures, eyeing the 50-day MA at $1,164.

Fresh York Governor signs new rules for private listings into law, Compass praises it
