⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest York’s governor has joined the growing lists of state lawmakers enacting laws to govern the use of private listing networks.
  • On Friday, Governor Kathy Hochul signed Senate Bill S10274, also known as the “Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listings Act,” into law, just seven days after it was delivered to her desk.
  • The legislation was first introduced in mid-March before going on to pass the Assembly in late May and the state Senate on June 1, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest York’s governor has joined the growing lists of state lawmakers enacting laws to govern the use of private listing networks.

On Friday, Governor Kathy Hochul signed Senate Bill S10274, also known as the “Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listings Act,” into law, just seven days after it was delivered to her desk.

The legislation was first introduced in mid-March before going on to pass the Assembly in late May and the state Senate on June 1, 2026.

The law requires residential listings to be publicly advertised or marketed on platforms that are accessible to the general public. According to the law, this means that the publication, platform or website the listing is advertised on does not require payment or for the consumer to work with a certain brokerage or agent in order to view the property information. Additionally, the law specifies that any licensed real estate broker or agent working with a buyer without limitation to a particular brokerage, franchise, or select group of licensees should also be able to view information about the listing.

Here’s how it will impact real estate professionals and brokerages:.

Despite this emphasis on ensuring listing information is easily accessible, the law does note that sellers who sign a state-provided standardized disclosure form explaining the risks and tradeoffs associated with non-public marketing, may withhold their listing from public marketing.

In the disclosure included in the text of the law, sellers must acknowledge that their property “may not be marketed or distributed outside the real estate brokerage that the listing agent is associated with through mass-marketing channels,” and that due to this, the seller understands that the reduced exposure of the property may lead to a reduction in the number of offers they receive, potentially negatively impacting their ability to sell the house.

Recent findings suggest that those who break this law can be fined up to $5,000. In addition, under the law, the Department of State may suspend or revoke a real estate professional’s license. The law is set to go into effect in late May 2027.

Bess Freedman, the CEO of New York City-based Brown Harris Stevens, a RealTrends Verified brokerage,  is celebrating the passage of the law.

“Buying a home shouldn’t depend on who you know or which brokerage you work with. I’m proud that New York is taking on private listing networks and making public marketing the standard,” Freedman wrote in an emailed statement. “Buyers deserve to see what’s available and choose who represents them. Sellers deserve the chance to reach the widest possible audience, and those who want privacy — a choice that has always existed — can still choose it with a clear understanding of what they may give up.”.

In addition to Freedman, Caroline Burton, the general manager of StreetEasy, which is owned by Zillow, is also applauding the news and thanking the state legislature for “putting consumers first.”.

“When homes are kept out of public view, Fresh Yorkers lose out, especially in a market where homes for sale are already scarce,” Burton wrote in an emailed statement. “Finding a home in the most challenging market shouldn’t depend on privilege, who you know or who you work with. In one of the biggest decisions in a person’s life, New Yorkers deserve an open and transparent marketplace so they can make an informed choice. This is a win for all buyers, sellers, and the agents who serve them.”.

Beyond these two firms, which had been vocal proponents of listing transparency, Compass International Holdings, which has been promoting its three-phased marketing proposal, which includes a private listing phase, is also praising the enacting of the law.

In a recent development, A Compass spokesperson told HousingWire that the fresh law “preserves homeowners’ right to choose how they market their homes,” which includes marketing the property through Compass’s See It First initiative. Compass rolled out See It First in September. The manufacturer said it is intended to expand inventory visibility for buyers, allow sellers to “test and learn” without public days on market and provide agents with an additional marketing lever.

“See It First early access homes comply with the new law and continue to give sellers flexibility in how and when they bring their homes to market,” a Compass spokesperson told HousingWire via email.

In enacting this law, Newly introduced York is joining Connecticut, Wisconsin and Washington in creating a law governing the public marketing of residential properties. New York’s law is similar to the ones passed in Connecticut and Wisconsin, both of which provide sellers the ability to opt-out of public marketing with a signed disclosure. The Washington law, however, does not include a pathway for sellers to opt-out of public marketing besides a health or safety concern. These laws are right now in effect in Connecticut and Wisconsin, with Washington’s law slated to go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Kia opened orders for two latest PV5 electric van variants, the PV5 Chassis and PV5 Cargo L2/H2, in the UK.

The PV5 is Kia’s first fully electric van from its Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) business. Built on Hyundai Motor’s dedicated modular skateboard platform, E-GMP.S, Kia can easily swap body styles to enable “limitless possibilities.”.

So far, the PV5 has mostly been available in Passenger and Cargo body styles with several different variations.

In a recent development, kia added the PV5 Chassis, an open-bed model that can be converted into just about anything. In the UK, Kia is offering conversions through TGS Automotive Group, including lightweight tipper, Dropside, and Box solutions.

The PV5 Chassis is available exclusively with the long-range 71.2 kWh battery in the UK, which Kia said could offer a potential WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km).

For reference, the PV5 Cargo L2/H1, which uses the same 71.2 kWh battery, offers a WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km). Other markets will also have a standard-range 51.1 kWh option.

The Chassis model is 4,610 mm long, 1,895 mm wide, and 1,935 mm tall, with a 2,995 mm wheelbase.

Its compact size and 5.5-meter turning radius, Kia noted, make it easy to maneuver in city streets, construction sites, and other tight work areas.

In a recent development, inside, the PV5 Chassis features two seats. Like other variants, it includes a 12.9″ navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display with standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

According to recent reports, the Chassis model supports DC fast charging up to 120 kW, enabling the battery to charge from 10% to 80% in about 30 minutes. Using an 11 kW AC supply, it takes about 6 hours and 30 minutes to charge from 10% to 100%.

Payload depends on the configuration. Kia said the Dropside offers a payload of up to 633 kg, while the Tipper can carry 561 kg.

In the UK, the PV5 Chassis is now on sale from £32,916 ($43,400) on the road, including the expected £5,000 ($6,700) UK Zero Emission Van Grant.

However, it’s an “incomplete vehicle,” as Kia describes it. The converted PV5 Dropside is priced from £40,110 ($53,500) on the road, including the ZEVG, while the PV5 Tipper starts at £41,310 ($55,000).

Kia also released the larger PV5 Cargo L2/H2 in the UK. The latest variant is 4,695mm long, 1,895mm wide, and 2,200mm high, with a 2,995mm wheelbase.

The taller roof opens up an internal cargo-area height of 1,815mm. It also offers a greater load capacity than the L1/H1 and L2/H2, with 5.2 cubic meters.

According to recent reports, it’s available in three- and four-door configurations with the choice of two or three seats. The three-door versions have a maximum payload of 630 kg, while the four-door models have dual sliding doors and offer a payload of up to 600 kg. Both versions can tow up to 1,500 kg.

Like the Chassis model, the PV5 Cargo L2/H2 is available in the UK exclusively with the 71.2 kWh battery, which provides a WLTP range of up to 239 miles.

Inside, it features the same setup as the other PV5 variants, including a 12.9″ touchscreen navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display.

The base PV5 Cargo L2/H2 Essential two-seat starts at £35,016 ($46,700), on the road, including ZEVG.

The article explains how printing methods, fabric choices, and order size affect apparel quality, durability, and production costs.

BUFFALO, N.Y., Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- How do businesses decide which custom apparel printing method best suits their project? HelloNation has published an article that answers the question by outlining the differences between screen printing and other common methods of printing custom business apparel and promotional shirts.

According to recent reports, the article featuring Kernell Miller of Buffalo, Fresh York, explains that screen printing remains one of the most widely used methods for business apparel because of its durability and consistent color. According to the article, screen printing works by pressing ink through a mesh screen directly onto garments, creating bold graphics that hold up well through repeated washing and everyday wear. This process is commonly used for promotional shirts, company uniforms, and large event orders.

The HelloNation article notes that screen printing becomes more cost-effective as order quantities increase. Since each color in a design generally requires its own screen setup, larger apparel runs help spread those setup costs across more garments. The article explains that many organizations choose screen printing for repeat commercial orders because it ensures consistent quality across every shirt in the batch.

In a recent development, the article also reviews several other custom shirt printing methods that may better suit smaller or more detailed projects. Direct-to-garment printing is a digital process capable of reproducing highly detailed artwork, gradients, and photographic images without the extensive setup required by traditional screen printing. The article explains that direct-to-garment printing can be especially useful for limited-run orders or for businesses that need only a small quantity of shirts.

Recent findings suggest that heat transfer printing is another option discussed in the article. According to the piece, heat transfer printing works well for specialty garments and performance fabrics that may not respond as effectively to traditional ink applications. The article describes how businesses often compare heat transfer printing with other custom apparel printing methods when working with athletic wear or materials that require flexibility and lightweight graphics.

Recent findings suggest that the HelloNation article emphasizes that design complexity plays a major role in selecting a printing process. Screen printing is preferred for simple logos, bold graphics, and large solid-color areas. At the same time, the article explains that direct-to-garment printing may offer advantages when designs feature intricate details or numerous color transitions that are difficult to reproduce with traditional screen-printing methods.

Industry observers note that fabric selection is also identified as an key consideration. The article explains that screen printing performs especially well on cotton garments and cotton blends, while some digital and specialty methods are designed for polyester or moisture-wicking materials. If you are ordering promotional shirts or employee uniforms, please evaluate fabric compatibility before committing to a large production order.

Industry observers note that the article further explains that production schedules and project budgets often influence the final decision. Smaller apparel orders may incur higher setup costs with screen printing, while digital methods can reduce preparation time and support faster turnaround times. The article notes that businesses comparing custom apparel printing services in Buffalo, NY often review production capabilities, previous work samples, and garment recommendations before selecting a provider.

Throughout the article, Custom Apparel Expert Kernell Miller explains that there is rarely a single printing solution that works for every project. Instead, businesses are encouraged to compare screen printing, direct-to-garment printing, and heat transfer printing based on artwork details, garment type, order size, and overall budget. The article concludes that understanding these differences helps companies make more practical decisions when ordering business apparel and promotional shirts.

Notably, the data further demonstrates that the metric has surpassed the previous reading of 2.09 recorded on July 6, marking a five-month high in XRP’s supply shortage index.

It is crucial to note that readings above +2 are a strong indication of severely tightened supply, which means that the amount of XRP available on the exchange has decreased significantly.

While negative readings often mean the opposite, this means that XRP has witnessed a sharp reversal from the supply level seen on September 27.

At the time, the index stood at -1.5 while XRP traded above $1.50, signaling an abundance of XRP on Binance. This means that more tokens were available for trading during the period, which potentially added to selling pressure.

While that is no longer the case, the latest data demonstrates that the XRP supply index has jumped by 3.9 points in just 53 days, moving from supply abundance to severe supply tightness in just about two months.

This typically suggests that XRP is being aggressively moved out of exchanges despite its prolonged price weakness, potentially driving a rebound in the demand for XRP, which could eventually trigger a price recovery.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon $AMZN has agreed to acquire the technology behind AI startup Decart, along with its founding team, for about $7.5 billion, according to Bloomberg.

Industry observers note that the purchase covers the Decart Optimization Stack, a software tool built to help AI models perform well on varied kinds of hardware, as well as Decart's researchers and engineers, according to Bloomberg. Amazon made the announcement on its company blog Monday. Amazon is not buying Decart's AI models.

According to recent reports, decart's website describes the stack as software that runs workloads on Google $GOOGL TPUs, Amazon's Trainium AI chips and Nvidia $NVDA GPUs. The company indicates the stack also powers its own models, as well as outside language models and agentic workloads.

Decart began collaborating with Amazon last year and has already put some of its models on Trainium, according to Bloomberg. The startup dates to 2023, when a trio of Israeli engineers — Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev — released it. It also makes AI models for editing video as it streams and for simulating real-world physics.

Industry observers note that amazon CEO Andy Jassy plans to start offering Trainium chips next year to other companies that build data centers, according to Bloomberg. Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud customers can already use the chips. Amazon has been trying to make Trainium simpler for customers to adopt, and it pitches the chip as a competitor to the Nvidia hardware behind most AI models.

Industry observers note that crypto Briefing put the deal at $7 billion to $7.5 billion. Crypto Briefing also says the price could be paid through a mix of cash, stock and deferred installments tied to performance, and that the founders have committed to remain at Amazon for five years. Crypto Briefing had reported that Amazon was expected to unveil the deal during AWS re:Invent on Nov. 30.

It has been revealed that decart declared a $300 million funding round in May, led by Radical Ventures. The round valued the company at about $4 billion, according to Crypto Briefing.

Decart held talks about a sale to Anthropic for about $6 billion, according to Bloomberg.

Amazon has been expanding its custom chip work on several fronts. In September, AWS agreed to license chip design technology from Synopsys $SNPS in a deal valued at more than $1 billion, the companies said. Jassy has raised the prospect of selling chip racks to outside customers. Annualized revenue from Amazon's Trainium, Graviton and Nitro chip lines is roughly $20 billion.

Breaking: Tesla tuner Unplugged offers to take over Cybertruck production

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, unplugged Performance, the biggest name in Tesla aftermarket tuning, wants to keep the Cybertruck alive.
  • It comes just four days after Elon Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around mid-2027, with the truck selling at roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year Tesla planned for.
  • UP posted the pitch on X as “an open offer to Tesla.” The tech giant says it fully supports putting Cybercab first and would run Cybertruck production “at no cost to Tesla’s floor space, headcount, or focus.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, unplugged Performance, the biggest name in Tesla aftermarket tuning, wants to keep the Cybertruck alive. The manufacturer publicly offered on Tuesday to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands, funded by a consortium of investors.

It comes just four days after Elon Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around mid-2027, with the truck selling at roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year Tesla planned for.

UP posted the pitch on X as “an open offer to Tesla.” The tech giant says it fully supports putting Cybercab first and would run Cybertruck production “at no cost to Tesla’s floor space, headcount, or focus.”.

It has been revealed that in exchange, Tesla would collect a license fee plus FSD and Robotaxi network revenue on every vehicle built. UP even offered to let Cybercab get first call on battery cells. “We’ll wait our turn,” the tech giant wrote.

UP founder Ben Schaffer made it clear that he supports Tesla’s all-in move to autonomy, but he wants to keep the Cybertruck program alive.

And it isn’t stopping at the pickup. UP says it would build the Cybertruck, a three-row “CyberSUV,” and an unmanned “CyberCargo” hauler. Two vehicles Tesla has sometimes referenced, but they were never unveiled.

According to recent reports, the post passed 240,000 views within hours, and the replies are mostly Cybertruck owners and Tesla shareholders begging Musk to say yes. Neither Musk nor Tesla had publicly responded at the time of writing.

UP has a lot riding on this. It sells an entire Cybertruck product line, the UP Invincible lift and armor kits, and it has scored several contracts to turn Cybertrucks into police vehicles for law enforcement agencies. CEO Ben Schaffer once described the company’s purpose as doing “the things that Tesla maybe wants to do, but doesn’t have the bandwidth to do.” This is that idea taken to its extreme.

Recent findings suggest that musk framed the Cybertruck’s end as a space problem. He said Tesla needs to “make room for increased Cybercab production.”.

Recent findings suggest that if the Cybertruck program was successful, Tesla wouldn’t be killing it. Tesla also produces Model Ys at Giga Texas, and it is not shutting that down to make room for Cybercab.

As we reported when Tesla unveiled the wind-down, that explanation doesn’t hold up. Giga Texas has more than 10 million square feet of floor space, the Cybertruck line runs at about a quarter of its 125,000-unit installed capacity, and Texas had only a few hundred Cybercabs registered as of late October.

The real problem is buyers. Tesla delivered 8,295 “Other Models” in Q3, and we estimated 7,000 to 8,000 of those were Cybertrucks, a pace of about 30,000 trucks a year. That was a good quarter by Cybertruck standards.

Sources indicate that even that number flatters it. S&P Global Mobility data highlighted SpaceX bought 1,279 Cybertrucks in Q4 2025, about 18% of US registrations that quarter. Tesla also tried a cheaper RWD trim, killed it, rolled out a $60,000 AWD version, then raised prices by $5,000 in August. None of it fixed demand.

I’ll give UP credit for this: the offer calls Musk’s bluff. If the Cybertruck is really dying because Cybercab needs the room, here’s someone volunteering to take the line off Tesla’s plate. Problem solved.

Of course, it’s more complicated than that.

There are many ways this could fail or never happen in the first place, but there’s also a slight possibility that makes this possible.

Sources indicate that first off, the backlash is real. If you look on social media and forums, yes, most of the discussion is about how Cybertruck is a failure, and Elon is lying about why Tesla is killing it, but there’s also a serious group of people, especially Cybertruck owners, who are genuinely upset that Tesla is killing the program because they love their trucks.

Most people have never driven a Cybertruck, but the steer-by-wire makes it a very addictive vehicle to drive, and even though the price is high, the value proposition for the specs is not bad compared to the very limited options for electric pickup trucks.

In other words, I wouldn’t necessarily bet against this effort, especially if they add an SUV variant and show the program some love with some tweaks here and there.

Sources indicate that I could see a group of wealthy Cybertruck fans pooling money under Unplugged to make this happen, but getting Tesla to agree could be hard. It’s not unheard of for an automaker to sell a vehicle program to a dealer, like the Lotus Seven and Studebaker Avanti, but it would be a first at this scale.

Who is singing up to light their cash on fire? There is just no way that would work. Unless Tesla just gave them the designs and tooling. Then they are stuck the same problem with who is their market. There are 3 ev trucks coming that are cheaper better and more practical. Likey 3 or 4 more by the end of the decade.

You could make sense of it by looking at UP to Tesla as AMG to Mercedes. It’s not too massive a stretch, considering UP isn’t just your average Tesla tuner. It even worked with the automaker on its own version of the Model S Plaid.

If UP were to become for Tesla what AMG has become for Mercedes, it could make some sense for the company to run a separate vehicle program that started under Tesla, but even as I write this, I realize that there’s very little chance this will happen.

But I wish them the best of luck, and I would be happy to see the Cybertruck live on.

Your Business Is Busy. But Is It Actually Growing? Ask These 4 Questions to Find Out.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Industry observers note that A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten.
  • Sources indicate that I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Industry observers note that A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he noted, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

Sources indicate that I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a tech giant.

We tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

According to recent reports, I think about Jack’s line a lot this time of year, because the fourth quarter makes business owners a little crazy. The year is almost over, you’ve got revenue goals to hit, budgets to review, and everyone’s already asking about your aims for next year. For a lot of founders, the natural response is to put their heads down and work harder. I’ve done it plenty of times myself, and I’ve learned that a lot of that extra effort goes into motion that never turns into progress.

It has been revealed that I’ve spent most of my career working with entrepreneurs building businesses in smaller markets. They know exactly when payroll hits, and they’re building their companies without millions of dollars in outside investment. For them, time is as tight as cash. A business like that can stay incredibly busy for years while nothing really changes.

So before the year wraps up, it’s worth asking a few uncomfortable questions to make sure your time and effort are actually moving you forward.

Revenue is key. I’m certainly not going to argue otherwise. But revenue alone can hide a lot. You can grow sales while your margins shrink. You can bring in newly introduced customers who are a nightmare to serve, or hire a bunch of people and add services only to discover you’ve built a more complicated version of the business you already had. I’ve watched founders post record sales and still end the year with less cash and less freedom than they started with.

Recent findings suggest that before you set another ambitious revenue target, look at what your growth is actually producing. Are you more profitable? Is your team getting stronger? Are your customers happier? Is the business becoming less dependent on you? Those questions will tell you a lot more about whether you’re building something that lasts.

Entrepreneurs are idea people. We love trying new things, whether it’s a new campaign or some shiny piece of software that promises to change everything (cough, cough, AI). I’m guilty of it, too. At some point, though, we have to be honest about the difference between what we enjoy doing and what moves the business forward.

Industry observers note that take marketing. You might spend hours making social media content because you enjoy it, while most of your best customers come from referrals. Or you might be convinced a particular service is your bread and butter, only to find out a less exciting offering is generating most of your profit. The numbers don’t always tell the story we want to hear.

In a recent development, so figure out where your best customers are coming from and what they’re buying. A spreadsheet and an honest hour will get you most of the way there. And if you identify something that’s working, do more of it.

This might be my favorite question, because it’s where founders find the quickest wins.

Sources indicate that every business picks up habits over the years: Meetings that made sense two years ago, reports nobody reads, software nobody logs into, services that stay on the menu because they’ve always been there. Individually, none of these seem like a massive deal. Added up, they eat a surprising amount of time and money, and they eat your attention, which might be the most valuable thing a founder has.

Look at what your team spends time on every week and ask a simple question: If we were starting this business today, would we still do it this way? If the answer is no, why are you doing it now?

According to recent reports, I love setting goals. I’m a substantial believer in having a vision and building a plan to get there. I’ve also learned that a newly introduced calendar year has never solved an old problem for me. If your sales process is broken in October, a fresh set of goals in January won’t fix it. If you’re spending money on marketing that doesn’t work, a bigger budget just means you’ll waste more of it. And if you’re the bottleneck in every decision, adding more customers is going to make your life harder.

For the first several years of Bolt, I was in every meeting. That made sense when we were scrappy and fighting for every account. As we grew, I started getting in the way of the systems we’d built to run without me. Now the question I ask my team constantly is, “Do I have to be in this meeting?” Usually the answer is no, and the business runs better because of it.

In a recent development, you don’t have to overhaul the whole company all at once. Pick one or two things that would make a real difference, like improving your margins, simplifying an offer, documenting a process or finally handing off something you’ve held onto for too long. Then make those changes now, while you still have some time left in the year.

There’s nothing wrong with pushing hard to finish the year strong. I hope you hit every goal you’ve set. Just don’t get so locked in on a number that you lose sight of what you’re building. Most of us started our businesses to create opportunity and have some control over our time and our future, and a bigger revenue line doesn’t guarantee either one.

Jack was right that you can’t do both at once. So before you lock in next year’s number, ask yourself which season you’re in. If it’s a season to get bigger, run. If it’s a season to get better, give yourself permission to slow down and fix what’s underneath. Either way, choose it on purpose.

In a recent development, A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he noted, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a firm.

It has been revealed that we tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

HOUSTON, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ours Privacy, the HIPAA-compliant marketing and analytics platform built by healthcare marketers for healthcare marketers, today rolled out custom dashboards to its Advanced Analytics Suite. Alongside a series of expert-built dashboards covering the metrics teams rely on most, healthcare marketers now have full flexibility to build their own dashboards and combine the exact reports they need in one customizable view. Each dashboard runs on Ours Privacy's own secure infrastructure, covered by a Business Associate Agreement (BAA), so teams can quickly and easily build the exact views they need without relying on a technical data team or separate analytics tool.

Build the exact dashboard your team needs.

Recent findings suggest that dashboards can be built around any visitor or event a team tracks across the Ours Privacy platform, from web events like page views or form starts through to backend events like tracked calls or attended appointments. Teams can query by any property, break results down by source, device, or campaign, and combine Insights, Funnels, Journeys, and Session Replays in a single view. Teams can even build their own attribution reports, spanning every channel and both frontend and backend events, and set their own conversion windows rather than relying on hard-coded definitions.

It has been revealed that every healthcare marketing team is different, and Ours Privacy is purposefully designed to meet each one where it is. Teams can jump directly into pre-built dashboards, chosen by Ours Privacy's healthcare marketing experts and ready to use as soon as the team goes live on the platform. Teams that want to explore custom options can start with seven Analytics Recipes, step-by-step intends for dashboards such as bookings by service line, newly introduced-patient demand by channel, patient access, and new-patient growth.

Build dashboards with AI and connect them to existing tools.

Teams that know exactly what they need can build every dashboard from scratch to their exact specifications, and teams that work with AI don't have to build anything by hand. Through the Ours Privacy MCP server, REST API, and other connectors, teams can build dashboards with AI and connect to the business intelligence tools they already use, on their terms and with the permissions they set.

It has been revealed that "Nothing about healthcare marketing is one-size-fits-all," said Tyler Zey, co-founder and chief technology officer of Ours Privacy. "Reporting shouldn't be, either. It's key that teams are able to own, query, and shape their own data without having to send it through a patchwork of other tools.".

Share results with leadership in one click.

With a single click, any dashboard can be converted into a full-screen presentation or branded PDF, so healthcare marketers can share the data trends their executive and legal teams want to see without having to manually configure spreadsheets.

Trust your data's accuracy and privacy.

According to recent reports, "Healthcare marketers shouldn't have to trade away the reporting flexibility they know from tools like GA4 to protect patient privacy," stated Adam Putterman, co-founder and chief revenue officer of Ours Privacy. "With custom dashboards in Ours Privacy's Advanced Analytics Suite, they get both plus capabilities GA4 was never built to offer, like Session Replays and Heatmaps, all wrapped into the same platform.".

Custom dashboards join other recent additions to the Ours Privacy platform, including the AI Assistant, which answers questions about performance and setup in plain language and is covered by the customer's BAA, and Mobile Analytics for iOS, Android, and React Native apps.

Ours Privacy is a HIPAA-compliant customer data platform (CDP) and marketing platform built by healthcare marketers for healthcare marketers. The platform is trusted by leading health systems, digital health companies, and national medical brands to modernize their marketing while navigating a rapidly evolving privacy environment. Ours Privacy integrates with major channels including Google Ads, Meta Ads, DSPs, EHRs, scheduling platforms, and data warehouses. Learn more at oursprivacy.com.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella opened his Ignite keynote Tuesday in San Francisco by addressing the elephant in the room: the global Outlook outage that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries last week.

Before getting to Copilot, agents or any of the event’s news, Nadella mentioned the outage was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure has become as “the dial tone for the world.”.

“We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” he said. “And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve.”.

The line drew applause from the crowd, interrupting Nadella as he moved to thank the IT pros in the audience who kept their own organizations running through the outage.

According to recent reports, it was a brief acknowledgment, and he didn’t go into what went wrong. Microsoft’s preliminary report blamed a bug in a fix it began rolling out in July, which its own automatic rerouting spread until most of the servers in a key Microsoft 365 gateway stopped responding. A final report is due Nov. 20.

Sources indicate that from there, Nadella moved on to the main show. Watch the keynote below, and see updates here.

Latest Update: It’s that time again – Honda needs to roll out an electric Super Cub

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every few years, I apparently feel compelled to remind Honda that it is sitting on what could be one of the easiest home runs in the electric motorcycle industry: just make an electric Super Cub already.
  • Sources indicate that I’m not talking about an electric scooter vaguely inspired by the Super Cub.
  • Sources indicate that the Honda Super Cub is arguably the most successful motor vehicle ever created, with well over 100 million produced since its introduction in 1958.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every few years, I apparently feel compelled to remind Honda that it is sitting on what could be one of the easiest home runs in the electric motorcycle industry: just make an electric Super Cub already.

Sources indicate that I’m not talking about an electric scooter vaguely inspired by the Super Cub. Not another futuristic concept with swoopy bodywork and a name that looks like a Wi-Fi password. I mean an actual honest-to-goodness Honda Super Cub, except electric.

The formula is already sitting right there.

Sources indicate that the Honda Super Cub is arguably the most successful motor vehicle ever created, with well over 100 million produced since its introduction in 1958. It’s still in continuous production today.

Recent findings suggest that and a huge part of that success comes down to how approachable the thing is. It isn’t supposed to be intimidating, excessively powerful, or particularly complicated. It’s simple, practical transportation wrapped in one of the most recognizable two-wheeler designs ever created.

In other words, it’s practically begging to become electric.

Sources indicate that the beauty of the bike is how simple and timeless it is, with the appearance barely changing in nearly 7 decades. And with the design freedom that electric drivetrains provide, upgrading the cute little bike to an electric future would be a walk in the park for Honda’s engineers.

An in-wheel motor would be a simple, cheap solution that frees up even more space in the body for batteries.

And Honda wouldn’t need some enormous battery capable of highway touring. Give an electric Super Cub enough battery for perhaps 50-60 miles (80-95 km) of real-world urban riding, a motor capable of roughly 50-60 mph (80-95 km/h), and simple Level 1 charging from a normal wall outlet. As a city runabout or a beachside cruiser, those middle-of-the-road specs would be perfect.

Recent findings suggest that even better, make the battery removable. Honda already has its Mobile Power Pack e: swappable battery system used in various electric two-wheelers, and an electric Super Cub would be an incredible platform to expand it.

The resulting bike could hit an unusually sweet spot.

There are millions of people riding electric bicycles today who will eventually want something faster, but don’t necessarily want a 500-pound (220 kg) electric motorcycle capable of hitting 120 mph (200 km/h). An electric Super Cub would be a natural next step: light, unintimidating, easy to ride, cheap to operate, and fast enough to actually function as a real urban vehicle.

It would also be one of the rare electric motorcycles that could appeal to people who aren’t necessarily looking for an “electric motorcycle.” An electric version is in such high demand that companies specialize in retrofit kits to convert classic Cubs into EVs.

It has been revealed that the Super Cub already has decades of cultural cachet. It’s cute. It’s useful. It’s nostalgic without feeling ancient. It’s the kind of motorcycle that can appeal equally to a lifelong rider and someone who has never considered owning a motorcycle before.

Recent findings suggest that and perhaps most importantly, Honda could actually sell the thing globally. The same basic electric Super Cub could work in dense European cities, throughout Asia, and in American cities and suburbs. It doesn’t need to win spec-sheet battles. It just needs to be affordable, reliable, and unmistakably a Super Cub.

In a recent development, my mum's old Honda-50 (the original cub, early 70's) had a tank that held less than a gallon of petrol. Range was realistically about 50 miles, but no-one even thought about that, it never ran out.

She traded for a honda-90, then a bunch of other stuff, I miss that 90, even now.

But the point is that range is not the concern, very few trips on these are more than 10 - 15 miles, say 30km round-trip.

But the real range, on a battery vehicle, is only about 2/3 of the claim,.

so if the claim is 80, it'll maybe do 55?

Thats enough, if it has the zip to handle traffic, and cruise at 45 - 50mph.

Honda has already shown that it understands the importance of electrifying small two-wheelers. It’s even made a token gesture with a Cub-like e-scooter in China. But there’s a difference between making another electric scooter and electrifying perhaps the most famous small motorcycle ever made.

So here I am once again, Honda.

Recent findings suggest that you’ve got the name. You’ve got the design. You’ve got the batteries. You’ve got the manufacturing scale.

Just put all the pieces together and give us the electric Super Cub already. The world is waiting, and will thank you.

Bitcoin (BTC), the world’s largest cryptocurrency, is flashing a major, ‘scary’ technical signal that was absent even during its last major crashes in February and June 2026.

The flagship coin has crashed to a fresh 4.5-month low amid persistent institutional outflows totaling billions from cryptocurrency exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

According to recent reports, $BTC hasn't formed a higher high for 16 consecutive days now. This didn't even happen during the Feb 2026 and June 2026 crashes. https://t.co/I6IPmdueEc.

In a recent development, bitcoin has failed to form a higher high for the past 16 days. This is a very long stretch, one that was absent during Bitcoin’s February and June crashes.

According to recent reports, A higher high, in the context of technical analysis, is formed when an asset’s price reaches a latest high point above its previous swing high. The absence of higher highs signals that buyers are having a hard time taking back control of the market.

The latest Bitcoin price action adds further to concerns surrounding the future of the flagship cryptocurrency.

Earlier today, BTC crashed to $61,225, its lowest price point in around four and a half months.

Bitcoin's failure to create higher highs despite several attempts to recover shows that selling pressure remains quite high.

Industry observers note that nevertheless, this technical pattern of 16 days without a higher high does not necessarily spell more pain for Bitcoin. If the cryptocurrency can decisively push above recent resistance zones, it may be a sign that buyers are starting to make a comeback.

Bitcoin is facing persistent withdrawals of huge amounts of money from U.S.-based spot Bitcoin ETFs.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) witnessed its biggest-ever daily net outflow on Nov. 19.

The crypto fund suffered a whopping $541.1 million in net withdrawals on the day. At the same time, total net outflows from U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs amounted to around $582.3 million across the entire market.

According to recent reports, more alarmingly, the fresh wave of withdrawals brings cumulative net outflows from U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs to around $3.47 billion so far this November.

The ETFs have seen negative net flows on 12 of the first 14 trading days of the month.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that now on Kickstarter, the FlexPilot dash cam combines flexible camera placement with a 12-inch, 1,500-nit display. Four-camera early-bird packages start at $569.

In a recent development, DALLAS, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Wolfbox, a leader in dash cams and automotive electronics, has rolled out the Wolfbox FlexPilotâ¢ dash cam on Kickstarter. FlexPilot is the world's first off-road mirror dash cam with four customizable camera mounting positions, giving off-roaders more control over what they can see from the driver's seat. The FlexPilot's QuadFlexâ¢ system lets drivers install up to four cameras almost anywhere on a vehicle or trailer, with all four channels streaming live to a 12-inch rearview mirror touchscreen display.

Standard dash cams only record the view through the front and rear windows. This might be fine for some city drivers, but off-roaders driving down a rocky trail will rapidly find that the view below the front bumper is what they actually need. Similarly, travelers often wish they could better monitor the lengthy blind spots on larger RVs, or keep an eye on a trailer hitch and the rear of a towed camper.

FlexPilot was designed to solve these problems. Instead of working around fixed camera positions, FlexPilot lets drivers choose what types of cameras are used and where they're mounted, customizing their very own camera system so that it is suited to their vehicle and the way they use it.

Custom views. Uncover the unseen.

The QuadFlex system supports up to four cameras, and there are five types of cameras to choose from: a 4K front camera, a 4K Flex camera and 1080p exterior, side and cabin cameras. The front, rear and Flex cameras sport Sony IMX678 STARVIS 2 sensors for excellent low-light visibility. A setup can combine up to two 4K and two 1080p cameras.

According to recent reports, when navigating a rock crawl or V-ditch, drivers care most about underbody clearance and the positions of individual tires. To keep an eye on these views, FlexPilot cameras can be mounted on the front bumper, on a fender or even under the chassis. With driveshaft repairs running from $1,500 to $4,000, it pays to see the trail ahead before committing to a line, especially in remote areas.

Sources indicate that towing calls for a different set of views. A camera near the hitch helps the driver line up more easily when connecting a trailer. A camera installed on the back of a trailer gives a view of a campsite when backing in. On an RV, a side-mounted camera can give a different blind spot view that regular side mirrors cannot match. The Flex camera can be connected to the driver's choice of 21.3-, 32.8- and 49.2-foot (6.5-, 10- and 15-meter) cables to accommodate different RV and trailer installations.

The real-time mirror display is similarly flexible. Drivers can use the display as a regular rearview mirror when needed and switch to any single camera feed when approaching an obstacle. They can even display multiple views, including all four channels at once.

For drivers filming their trips, an optional cabin camera can record passengers and commentary alongside exterior footage. The cabin camera is sold separately.

Similar factory camera packages can cost more than $2,000. Wolfbox offers a lower cost aftermarket option for drivers who want extra views for trail driving or towing, with four-camera FlexPilot early-bird packages priced at $569.

Clear views at all times of day.

It has been revealed that having all those cameras makes little difference if the driver can't see the display. An exposed stretch of trail can cast glaring sunlight onto the screen, only to transition to a wooded section within a few yards, plunging the cabin into darkness. Wolfbox designed the FlexPilot with a 12-inch Adaptive Displayâ¢ that adjusts to these changes, reaching up to 1,500 nits in daylight and dimming in the dark.

FlexPilot has the brightest display of all Wolfbox dash cams, with peak brightness comparable to some flagship smartphone and television screens. The display limits reflections and ghosting in direct light and reduces glare at night, giving drivers a clear view in most lighting conditions without an overly bright or too-dim screen hampering their vision.

FlexPilot also includes an advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) with lane departure and forward collision warnings, a lead-vehicle start reminder and blind-spot detection, making the system also an ideal companion for everyday driving. Drivers have access to voice control, GPS and dual-band Wi-Fi 6, with support for memory cards up to 1 TB.

Fitting FlexPilot to the vehicle.

FlexPilot is designed for most SUV, pickup, trailer and RV setups, including popular off-road vehicle models from Jeep, Ford, Toyota, and other brands.

Depending on the installation, drivers can use an OEM-style bracket, straps or a center-console base. A universal OEM bracket is sold separately for $29.

The Flex, rear, exterior and side cameras carry IP67 dust and water protection for installation on the outside of the vehicle.

Kickstarter packages and availability.

According to recent reports, the FlexPilot campaign opened on November 17, 2026, and runs through December 31, 2026. Kickstarter has selected it as a "Project We Love.".

Every package includes the 12-inch mirror display. Early-bird pledges start at $479 for DIY Basic, or $569 for either of the four-camera packages:.

Sources indicate that early-bird quantities are limited. All prices are in U.S. dollars. Estimated delivery in early spring 2027, with free U.S. shipping and an 18-month warranty. Additional cameras and accessories cost extra.

The campaign page includes off-road demonstrations and uncut prototype footage for a closer look at the system in use.

Back FlexPilot on Kickstarter:https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/wolfbox/wolfbox-flexpilot-multi-angle-monitoring-with-dash-cam.

Since 2019, Wolfbox has provided more than 2.5 million drivers across 94 countries with reliable dash cam technology and automotive solutions. Winner of awards from SEMA and TWICE, the brand has also expanded its driving ecosystem with the new GEARS line, bringing rugged bed covers, power steps, and high-output lighting to off-road enthusiasts.

For more information, visit wolfbox.com and gears.wolfbox.com.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am.
  • In a recent development, chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon.
  • Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club announced Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am.

In a recent development, chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a latest job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club announced Tuesday.

“His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer stated in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”.

Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation company toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the company’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

According to recent reports, chew mentioned his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

“In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”.

Chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he stated. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

The couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry. Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.

A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew said.

In a recent development, the job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he said.

Talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew remarked.

In a recent development, chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

On the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and said, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.

It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew notes he’s been doing a lot of lately.

In a recent development, “I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he noted. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”.

Chew is also working with players.

Industry observers note that he recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew remarked, and asked if they could do it every game.

The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox, was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew stated he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

Industry observers note that the bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew mentioned. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a big win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.

“It has to be approachable for folks,” he mentioned. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”.

It has been revealed that the Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.

“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he mentioned.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:43 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:43 am.
  • Sources indicate that seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech.
  • The department’s Arson/Bomb Squad is now using a Spot robot from Boston Dynamics, bought with a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that the Seattle City Council approved in April after a review of privacy and security risks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:43 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:43 am.

Sources indicate that seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog.

The department’s Arson/Bomb Squad is now using a Spot robot from Boston Dynamics, bought with a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that the Seattle City Council approved in April after a review of privacy and security risks. Bomb technicians can steer the robot from nearly a mile away to inspect suspicious devices, open doors and move possible explosives into safe containers, SPD mentioned in a blog post last week.

It’s a big upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily.

SPD also spelled out what Spot won’t do.

According to recent reports, the robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD noted a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition.

Sources indicate that the only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.”.

It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work.

Nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time.

Spot appears decidedly less cuddly.

According to recent reports, boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later.

The machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the company’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot.

Police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. Newly introduced York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash, then brought the robots back two years later.

Industry observers note that back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives.

And the robot won’t be getting a fresh name, SPD said, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”.

#144767. Alphabet, ServiceNow, Visa and Accenture are buying security to defend their core

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1432 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

Alphabet, ServiceNow, Visa and Accenture are buying security to defend their core

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1432 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, alphabet, ServiceNow, Visa and Accenture bought security companies to defend their core businesses.
  • For years, companies bought cybersecurity from specialist vendors the way they bought insurance: as a cost of doing business.
  • These buyers don't see security as a side business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, alphabet, ServiceNow, Visa and Accenture bought security companies to defend their core businesses. See what each deal buys and what is still a forecast.

For years, companies bought cybersecurity from specialist vendors the way they bought insurance: as a cost of doing business. That's changing. Some of the biggest buyers of security companies now are businesses whose main products are cloud computing, office software, card payments and consulting.

These buyers don't see security as a side business. They use it to make their core product harder to leave and harder to copy. A cloud provider that owns the tool protecting its cloud, or a payments network that owns the tool catching fraud, gives customers one more reason to stay.

Sources indicate that the catch, which the size of these deals can obscure, is timing. Each buyer pays now, but the return comes later, if it comes at all. Some of the payoff depends on customers adopting new tools across an entire network. Some depends on buyers getting their profit margins back after absorbing the companies they bought. And in at least one case, the deal hasn't even closed yet.

In a recent development, so the useful question isn't how massive each deal is. It's what the buyer gains by owning a security firm outright, and how long it'll take to find out whether the bet paid off.

24/7 Wall St. looked for the largest and most strategically important security acquisitions by companies outside the security industry. The buyers include a card network buying a company that studies how people type and swipe, a consulting giant moving into industrial security and a major cloud provider buying a company that protects workloads in the cloud. In each case, the buyer is spending on whatever it most needs to defend, and each deal below is judged on what it gains and how much of the payoff is still to come.

According to recent reports, google $GOOGL has finished buying Wiz. Now the question is whether it pays off. At $32 billion, Wiz is the biggest of these deals, and Google closed it on March 11, 2026, according to Cybersecurity Dive. The case for the price is that better security helps Google Cloud win more customer workloads, at a time when the business is booming: Google Cloud revenue grew 82% in the second quarter. Google is betting Wiz helps keep that growth going.

Sources indicate that but Wiz protects more than Google's cloud. It also secures customers on Amazon $AMZN Web Services, Microsoft $MSFT Azure and Oracle $ORCL Cloud, according to Cybersecurity Dive. That means Google is now a security vendor to companies running on its competitors' clouds.

Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, framed the deal in those broader terms. "With the addition of Wiz, we will provide customers with a comprehensive platform to secure their cloud and hybrid environments, as well as accelerate threat prevention, detection and response," Kurian remarked.

According to recent reports, that creates a measurement problem for investors. Security Google sells to a company running on Amazon's cloud won't show up as a workload moving to Google, so much of the deal's success may not appear in the cloud growth numbers investors usually watch.

Sources indicate that wiz also rounds out a security business Google had already built through Mandiant and its Chronicle security operations tools. Now Google can sell cloud protection, Mandiant consulting and security operations tools under one roof.

Whether it pays off depends on how many companies, including those on Amazon's and Microsoft's clouds, decide they want Google protecting them.

Recent findings suggest that serviceNow $NOW sells software that moves work through large companies, and it was selling security to its biggest customers before it bought a single security firm. Security was part of 16 of its 20 largest customer deals in the second quarter, according to 24/7 Wall St. In other words, its acquisitions followed demand that already existed.

ServiceNow then bought two companies to handle a security incident from start to finish. Veza makes tools that show and control who and what can reach a company's data, apps and AI agents, according to ServiceNow. Armis tracks nearly 7 billion devices. The bigger of the two deals, Armis, cost about $7.75 billion.

Both deals are recent. Veza closed on March 2, 2026, and Armis closed on April 20, after the first quarter ended. Any boost from Armis is still largely something ServiceNow expects rather than something it has shown.

The deal also comes with a cost. ServiceNow expects Armis to weigh on profit margins in fiscal 2026 and doesn't expect margin growth to return to normal until fiscal 2027. And some of Armis' revenue is less locked in than it looks, since some customers can cancel their contracts for convenience.

ServiceNow bought what its customers were asking for. Now it's paying in profits while it waits to see whether those customers stick around long enough to make it worthwhile.

According to recent reports, visa $V is buying security to protect the business it already runs. It's paying $2.4 billion for BioCatch to cut fraud losses in its payments network, according to 24/7 Wall St. The deal was declared in August and is expected to close by March 2027.

This isn't Visa turning into a security tech giant. It's buying a better way to block fraud on its own payments, building on its 2024 purchase of fraud detection firm Featurespace. BioCatch tracks how people type, tap and swipe, so a bank can flag an impostor even when they enter the right account details. Andrew Torre, Visa's president of value-added services, claims BioCatch will help Visa's clients catch fraud earlier, before any money moves.

For a payments network, every fraud stopped before checkout is one less bad transaction that could cost Visa the trust of cardholders and banks.

Recent findings suggest that the catch is reach. BioCatch counts roughly 350 banks as customers, according to company figures reported by CNBC, while Visa connects nearly 14,500 financial institutions. Visa only gets the fraud savings it wants if many more of those institutions sign on.

The size of the problem explains the price tag. Scams and account takeovers cost more than $1 trillion worldwide each year, according to a Visa estimate reported by CNBC, far more than what Visa is paying. And BioCatch isn't pretending the industry has it under control. "The reality is, as a society and industry, we are not winning this fight," the company wrote in a blog post about the deal.

Visa is betting it can get ahead of a kind of fraud that even the manufacturer it's buying notes the industry is losing to.

Accenture $ACN spent roughly $4.18 billion to add industrial security products to a business that mostly makes money from consultants, according to 24/7 Wall St. It's hardly new to security: Its cybersecurity business already brings in around $10 billion in revenue, according to Silicon Republic.

It has been revealed that what's new is the target. Operational technology security protects the systems that run factories, plants and other industrial operations, not office computers. Here, Accenture wants to own the tools instead of advising clients on tools other companies make.

Julie Sweet, Accenture's CEO and chair, says clients across industries want to get ahead of attacks and treat security as one coordinated effort. Owning the products lets Accenture sell that as a single package instead of stitching together tools from outside vendors.

Rather than folding the deals into its consulting practice, Accenture is building a separate product unit around Dragos. It now holds a majority stake in Dragos and owns runZero and NetRise outright. Dragos will keep running as its own business, and three executives from the two smaller companies are joining it, combining all three into one industrial security unit.

According to recent reports, worth noting: The $4.18 billion covers all three deals, and one of them is only a controlling stake. It's not the price of owning three companies in full.

Sources indicate that the price is a bet on growth, not current earnings. Accenture expected the three companies to bring in about $208 million in annual recurring revenue as of June 2026. That's small next to the security business Accenture already runs. Sweet herself expects a slow payoff, saying the deal "may not make as major a contribution ... in the first couple of years.".

Sources indicate that for now, what Accenture owns is a plan for an industrial security products business. The price will only look smart if that business gets big.

Recent findings suggest that privacy coins are poised to be among the biggest cryptocurrency stories of 2027, driven by growing concerns over financial surveillance, institutional adoption, and the future of digital privacy. This creates a compelling investment narrative. Google Gemini AI predicts that two projects, Monero (XMR) and Zcash (ZEC), will stand out, and it aims to forecast which will experience a significant price surge in 2027.

Both Monero and Zcash are established leaders in the privacy-focused cryptocurrency space, but they employ fundamentally different approaches to protecting customers’ financial information. Monero offers privacy by default, while Zcash seeks to balance financial confidentiality with greater accessibility for institutional investors.

Industry observers note that as a potential major crypto bull market approaches in 2027, investors may find two distinct opportunities for substantial returns. However, determining which option could deliver the biggest gains may yield surprising results.

Monero has long been considered the gold standard for transaction privacy. Unlike conventional cryptocurrencies, where transactions can be publicly inspected on a blockchain, XMR makes privacy an inherent feature of its network.

It has been revealed that it achieves this through ring signatures, Ring Confidential Transactions (RingCT), and stealth addresses, which conceal the sender, transaction amount, and recipient. Importantly, privacy is mandatory, not optional.

This gives Monero a compelling proposition as a digital cash alternative, especially as blockchain analytics grow more sophisticated and financial surveillance expands.

Recent findings suggest that however, that same characteristic creates a significant obstacle: regulatory scrutiny. Exchanges in several jurisdictions have restricted or removed XMR trading, potentially limiting access to a broader pool of investors.

Zcash takes a different approach, using zero-knowledge cryptography to enable shielded transactions while retaining the option of transparent transactions.

In a recent development, its shielded addresses let owners conceal transaction details, while viewing keys let them selectively disclose information to auditors or other authorized parties. This flexibility could prove particularly attractive to institutions that want privacy without completely sacrificing compliance.

The distinction could become increasingly vital as institutional investors look beyond Bitcoin and Ethereum for opportunities in specialized crypto sectors.

Recent findings suggest that privacy coins are already attracting attention beyond their traditional communities. Zcash has made considerable progress in positioning itself as a more institutionally accessible privacy network, with regulated investment products emerging and interest in its underlying technology growing.

Meanwhile, Monero continues to benefit from its established reputation, consistent privacy guarantees and decentralized architecture.

The broader investment narrative is also changing. As cryptocurrency adoption increases, more transactions become visible to blockchain analytics companies, incentivizing individuals and businesses to seek greater financial confidentiality.

However, the regulatory landscape could become a major obstacle in 2027. The EU’s Anti-Money Laundering Regulation is scheduled to apply from July 10, 2027, with restrictions covering crypto-asset accounts involving anonymity-enhancing coins.

Crucially, the legislation’s definition encompasses privacy features that operate either systematically or optionally. This means neither project can assume its architecture provides an exemption.

Looking beyond daily price fluctuations, the weekly and monthly charts will be particularly important in determining which cryptocurrency has the strongest potential heading into 2027.

For Monero, the key technical consideration is whether it can establish a sustained higher-high structure following its previous major market cycle. A successful retest of former resistance zones as support could lay the groundwork for another substantial move, particularly if capital rotates toward privacy-focused assets.

Recent findings suggest that XMR also benefits from a relatively predictable supply model. Its permanent tail emission produces 0.6 XMR every two minutes, with an inflation rate that gradually declines over time.

Zcash, meanwhile, has a more conventional fixed supply of 21 million coins, giving it a familiar scarcity narrative. Its longer-term technical outlook will depend heavily on whether it can maintain gains tied to its growing institutional profile and establish stronger historical support.

Both could benefit enormously from a broader cryptocurrency bull market, although ZEC’s previous outperformance means investors should also consider the possibility of profit-taking and deeper corrections.
