Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the tech giant prepares to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

It has been revealed that sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he remarked. “We have to take upcoming technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”.

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky stated. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Industry observers note that batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

Industry observers note that in August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

It has been revealed that the startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

Recent findings suggest that the tech giant has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round revealed in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently declared prepares for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky stated.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our firm’s history,” he said.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

“None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky remarked. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia rose roughly 30% when Jensen Huang returned as CEO. See how the move reached the Nasdaq, S&P 500 and bonds, and what risk remains.

Credit: Mariia Berezovsky / Unsplash.

Investors usually punish only one firm's shares when its chief executive is caught in a personal scandal. Jensen Huang's affair became a larger test: how much of the AI boom investors had tied to a single person. CNBC reports that Huang admitted on Nov. 8 to an extramarital affair. Within weeks, Nvidia $NVDA's board had put him back at the head of the company. The story soon stopped being about one executive's conduct. Investors began asking whether the world's most closely watched chip company could run without its founder, and nobody could answer that quickly.

When Nvidia's board reinstated Huang, it reversed its own position. The board had remarked it was not considering bringing him back, according to CNBC. Elon Musk, Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner all lobbied for Huang's return. A board that reverses itself while prominent outsiders press it to do so shows how much of Nvidia's worth its backers attach to one man.

Sources indicate that forbes set out to show five market effects of Nvidia's CEO coming back, from the bond market and the worry about leaning on a single leader to the major stock indexes. Not every effect points the same way. The gains reflect investors' relief that Huang is back, and the caveats reflect a dependence on him that his return leaves in place.

Industry observers note that nvidia $NVDA's own shareholders gave the clearest judgment on Jensen Huang's return, buying the stock until it had risen roughly 30%, according to Forbes. Investors had also sold sharply when he left. On Nov. 12, the day Huang announced he was leaving, investors drove the stock down as much as 14% during the session, CNBC reports, and they had cut the loss to 4.34% by the end of the day. Even at its worst point, the selling on his exit did not go as far as the buying on his return.

The size of the rally reflects the cost investors had expected to pay without him. Wall Street analysts had warned that shares could fall 20% if Huang departed, according to CNBC. When he came back, investors lifted the stock by more than that warned decline. Shareholders were paying for continuity, with a known decision-maker back in charge. They were not judging that the scandal didn't matter.

For two weeks, Nvidia $NVDA's worth depended on whether Huang would sit in the chief executive's chair. Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring him back, CNBC reports, and investors restored more than $1 trillion of the organization's value, according to Forbes. Investors were putting a price on having their founder in charge, and they valued his presence at a large share of what the company is worth.

The board did not make that decision from faith in Huang alone. Nvidia's falling shares were one reason the talks over his return moved faster, according to . The loss of value helped force the vote that won the value back. The board also offered investors an assurance when it declared the move, saying his reinstatement "poses no national security risk." The trillion dollars rests partly on that assurance and on pressure from a sliding stock, as much as on the board's view of Huang as a leader.

According to recent reports, huang's return brought enough relief to pull money out of the asset that investors treat as the safest place to hold it. Investors sold U.S. government debt to move money back into technology shares, according to Forbes, so one executive's reinstatement shifted money from the safe side of their holdings to the risky side.

Industry observers note that investors gave up a well-paid, low-risk holding to make that trade. The yield on the 10-year Treasury was 5.15% on Nov. 13 and 5.04% on Nov. 19, the last reading before Huang came back, according to Federal Reserve figures reported by FRED. A falling yield means rising prices, so investors were paying more for government debt during the week Nvidia $NVDA was without its founder. The selling after his return ran in the opposite direction. It also meant giving up a steady return of more than 5%, backed by the U.S. government, to own part of.

For now, investors have paid to keep Huang, and the cost is a stock whose value rises and falls with his fortunes.

According to recent reports, investors restored that value while the board's own inquiry into Huang remains open. CNBC reports that Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, which Nvidia's board hired for the investigation, is still carrying it out. The recovered value reflects investors' relief at his return rather than the outcome of that review.

Nvidia has its trillion dollars back, but it holds that value on terms that could change once Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz reports what it finds.

Credit: rc.xyz NFT gallery / Unsplash.

Industry observers note that investors carried their relief over Huang's return beyond Nvidia $NVDA's own stock and into the benchmarks meant to stand for the whole U.S. market. As AI shares recovered, investors pushed the Nasdaq $NDAQ up about 6% and the S&P 500 up about 4%, according to Forbes. Nvidia alone makes up about 6% of the S&P 500, according to CNBC. When investors bought back into one industry, with one organization at its center, they moved a gauge built to represent hundreds of companies. Someone who owns an S&P 500 fund to spread risk was partly betting on one founder's fate without choosing to.

The week Huang left, investors shifted money from Nvidia toward its chipmaking rivals. On Nov. 12, as Nvidia's shares slid, AMD $AMD and Broadcom $AVGO each closed up more than 5%, according to CNBC. At least some of that money stayed with AI chipmakers rather than leaving the industry. The later Nasdaq gain came as AI stocks recovered after Huang's return. That timing suggests investors were reacting to news about one company's leadership more than to a fresh view of AI or the economy.

Gains based on relief about a person are less steady than gains based on profits. "But, this stock is not going to trade on fundamentals ... for a while because you have the overhang of the investigations of leadership changes of potential departures," Stephanie Link, chief investment strategist at Hightower Advisors, noted, as reported by CNBC. Because the index gains came with that recovery in AI shares, the benchmarks now carry the same exposure to questions about Nvidia's leadership.

Anyone holding an index fund is now exposed to swings tied to who runs one company, for as long as those questions remain open.

Investors who move money this readily on news about one man's job can move it back just as readily if his position comes into doubt again. Huang's return was supposed to settle the question of founder risk, but it has tied even holders of government debt more closely to that risk.

In a recent development, bringing Huang back calmed investors, but it left Nvidia $NVDA just as dependent on him as before. Analysts remain concerned that the firm leans too heavily on one leader, according to Forbes. That concern has nothing to do with the affair. It is about how much of the company runs through a single person, and reinstating that person does nothing to reduce it.

It has been revealed that the warning came early, the day after Huang admitted the affair. On Nov. 9, Matt Bryson, managing director at Wedbush, told CNBC there was "key-person risk," the phrase investors use for a company whose fortunes depend on one executive. The board's reversal brought Huang back before investors could see how Nvidia would run under someone else, so the question Bryson raised was never answered.

Huang's return puts off the question of what Nvidia is without him, but it doesn't answer it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charles Hoskinson’s Cardano-linked privacy blockchain Midnight has inked a substantial initial deal with a Japanese payments manufacturer as it aims to make further inroads into traditional finance.

The news comes soon after a key breakthrough for Midnight in the United Kingdom, where Monument Bank started tokenizing customer deposits on the blockchain.

Per a Nov. 19 NADA NEWS report, Midnight Foundation President Fahmi Syed remarked the foundation had inked an MOU (memorandum of understanding) with a major Japanese payments company.

Syed did not name the firm. But the deal is a big one for Midnight’s bid to establish a presence in Japan’s financial services sector.

However, it is just an initial agreement, and no commercial services have been rolled out in Japan yet.

It is also worth noting that the Midnight Foundation is talking to some major Japanese banks and companies working with intellectual property and medical data.

According to Syed, he spent two days in Tokyo meeting with major financial institutions and other companies.

Japan has been a key market for Midnight, along with the United States.

According to Midnight Foundation Japan country manager Taro Kimura, Japan is the only Asian country where the foundation has a local representative on the ground.

Midnight has been eyeing Japan more keenly due to the country’s sizeable Cardano community.

The Japanese push comes hot on the heels of a historic development in the British banking sector.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 18, British financial institution Monument Bank started tokenizing retail customer deposits on Midnight. It is the first UK bank to launch such a product on a public blockchain.

The first phase of the venture involves up to £250 million in tokenized deposits. For this, the bank is offering customers a 12-month fixed annual interest rate of 5.2%.

Midnight employs zero-knowledge cryptography to safeguard sensitive transaction details, unlike traditional public blockchains. As a result, banks can meet compliance requirements while keeping their customers’ private information and transaction details out of public view.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that I run a global business called Brand of a Leader, which supports founders and executives in more than 12 countries by helping them build their visibility. When I first launched my business six years ago, all I had was a LinkedIn profile — no website and, naturally, no digital footprint of any kind yet.

And so our first few clients came through my network. By being active on LinkedIn and consistently sharing my perspective, I would stay top of mind with people who already knew me. When they needed support, or when someone in their own network did, I was the one who came to mind and was hired or recommended.

Recent findings suggest that today, I continue to use LinkedIn actively to generate clients, develop relationships and stay connected with my network. I’ve been on the platform for over 20 years, and throughout the years, I’ve heard people constantly complain about one thing: the algorithm. I always chuckle because the discourse is consistently the same, yet it’s presented as something new. Through all of my work and my extensive work supporting founders across the globe with their LinkedIn, I’ve seen how much people overindex on what to post, when to post and how to post, while overlooking something else that is likely even more key!

Recent findings suggest that here are the three mistakes I see founders make all the time. And I promise that if you fix those, you will see better results from this platform.

Obsession over what, when and how to post is real. Short posts or long posts? Daily or weekly? With a photo? Video? No media? What should I even write about? Those are undoubtedly key questions, yet there’s another one: What happens when someone reads your post, does become interested in learning more about you and then clicks on your profile?

My experience shows me that most founders don’t pay much attention to what’s actually on their profile. I know this because I constantly audit LinkedIn pages as part of the service that we provide at Brand of a Leader.

Too often, when I visit a LinkedIn profile, I find a bland banner or none whatsoever, and a short “About” section written in the third person. Whatever interest the person’s post may have piqued is swiftly lost when visiting their uninspiring profile.

Personally, I treat my profile as a landing page. And we do the same for our clients. For entrepreneurs, myself included, a well-designed LinkedIn page can be a practical alternative to a personal website when used thoughtfully.

Visit your profile, looking at it through the eyes of a potential client, and see what impression it would leave on them after spending a minute or two scrolling through it.

It has been revealed that one of the things we consistently convince our clients not to do is include calls to action in their posts. Salesy or overly promotional messages on founders’ profiles don’t make a great impression.

As a reader, I find that repeated prompts to book a call can make otherwise thoughtful writing feel overly promotional. I prefer to keep my content, and my clients’ content, conversational, expertise-building or humanizing. Yet, I do understand the importance of giving interested readers a clearly visible way to take the next step.

Instead of salesy calls to action in posts, I leverage the custom call-to-action button included with LinkedIn Premium Business. You can have it say anything that’s most relevant to you and your goals (for example, “Visit my website” or “Book a call”). This link will appear in your profile, just under your name and above the post that you write. That feels more elegant to me.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest mistakes I see founders make is treating LinkedIn as a broadcasting platform and not a social media platform. This is not only the quickest way to reduce the overall engagement of your content on LinkedIn, but it’s also not great for your positioning overall. When you only post and never engage, it positions you as a taker, not a giver, and also discourages people from further engaging with you.

At a minimum, you need to reply to people who took the time to comment on your posts. No, not only a “like” — an actual thoughtful reply. They have taken time to respond to something you shared. Read their contribution and respond to the substance of it.

In a recent development, and then ideally, extend that attention to other people’s content. Comment to share a relevant experience or ask a thoughtful question. If someone describes a challenge you have faced, explain what you learned. But don’t use AI. Generic, bland comments negatively impact your brand equity. Take 30 minutes to leave some authentic comments a couple of times weekly, and that consistency will compound over time.

According to recent reports, before publishing your next post, think about what interested readers will see on your profile if they click on it. Give them enough context to understand your expertise, an easy way to contact you and your attention when they engage in conversation with you.

In a recent development, before you hit publish again, take a look at LinkedIn’s newly introduced Small Business Playbook for practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to make sure your profile is ready when interested readers click through.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data indicates Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

In a recent development, according to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

It has been revealed that october was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

Sources indicate that the deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

In a recent development, NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

Industry observers note that as of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

According to recent reports, in October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who proposal to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

Industry observers note that in practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. People need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

According to recent reports, the September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

Recent findings suggest that that has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

Recent findings suggest that the useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too massive to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting fresh software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy, the organization’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how substantial we’re willing to dream.”.

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The tech giant has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy stated there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Sources indicate that annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The upcoming products take that approach further:.

According to recent reports, to decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Industry observers note that duffy remarked he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” remarked Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”.

In a recent development, both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise intends.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy stated.

Sources indicate that AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy stated many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The newly introduced products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Industry observers note that plenty of firm: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy noted. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”.

Industry observers note that bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy noted.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Recent findings suggest that pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy noted no launch in the company’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

It has been revealed that the business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy stated. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the organization, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy noted, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

About 40 of the tech giant’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy mentioned Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building latest products.

Sources indicate that despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the organization, Duffy said Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”.

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy remarked Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russia has finally opened its crypto market for retail customers as its central bank today enabled trading in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT for the general public. With the law signed by President Vladimir Putin, the Bank of Russia officially rolled out BTC, ETH, and USDT for public trading on domestic exchanges, beginning Nov. 17, 2026.

The fresh regulation, unveiled by the Bank of Russia last week, took effect today, Nov. 17. The move allows individual customers to purchase these assets through intermediaries, including brokers, exchanges, and authorized crypto marketplaces. This means ordinary investors can now buy up to 300,000 rubles ($3,700) in a year through a single broker, exchange, or asset manager, after passing a mandatory test.

Recent findings suggest that the announcement expands access to regulated crypto trading in the country and connects the assets with TradFi. This allows non-qualified investors to buy and trade BTC, ETH, and USDT directly through traditional exchanges and clearing systems.

However, qualified investors are not subject to such asset limits and trading restrictions.

The development points out that Russia has taken decisive action to deepen the integration of the crypto market with traditional finance. The debut indicates surging retail interest in cryptocurrency amid regulatory evolution.

It signals a strategic shift in how traditional exchanges handle digital assets. Accommodating retail clients signals growing confidence in the crypto market’s maturity. This highlights rising demand for coordinated exposure to crypto assets within Russia’s capital markets.

The announcement introduces new entry gateways that give retail investors organized access to the crypto market, redefining how these assets are traded locally and internationally.

In the past, crypto in Russia operated in a highly restrictive, complex regulatory environment. Now, the regulator is moving toward a balance between investor freedom and financial stability. In July, the central bank opened the door to crypto for companies to facilitate global trade. This month, it introduced upcoming legislation that allows retail investors to trade crypto within specified limits.

Toyota and Subaru’s latest electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.

The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.

Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.

Outside of Rivian, Toyota and Subaru are the only brands that have higher year-over-year EV sales in the US through the third quarter.

Combined, Toyota and Subaru have sold nearly 50,000 EVs through the first nine months of 2026, more than double compared to the same period last year.

It has been revealed that toyota alone has sold nearly 35,000 electric vehicles, up 183.4% YOY, while Subaru sold 14,630, up 46.7%. And that’s not even including the additional 12,676 sold under the Lexus brand, up 137.4% YOY.

While the two Japanese automakers were infamously slow to transition to battery electric vehicles, the timing worked in their favor.

According to recent reports, after launching the heavily updated bZ in late 2025, previously called the bZ4X, Toyota’s electric SUV suddenly became one of America’s most popular EVs. Through Q3, it was the fourth best-selling EV in the US, trailing only the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

Sources indicate that starting at $35,000, the Toyota bZ is one of the most affordable EVs in the US. It also offers up to 314 miles of range in the FWD Plus trim, which starts at $37,980.

Toyota and Subaru now each sell three electric SUVs, which share the same platform and technology.

With prices ranging from roughly $35,000 to about $45,000, Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, said (via Bloomberg) Toyota and Subaru’s new EVs are affordable and hit the “sweet spot” of the US car market.

Toyota also sells the smaller, sporty C-HR, starting at $37,080, and the larger, more rugged bZ Woodland, which starts at $45,380.

Subaru, on the other hand, sells the updated Solterra ($38,495, plus the smaller Uncharted ($34,995) and midsize Trailseeker ($39,995).

Karla Fisher, a Marine and retired engineer, told Bloomberg that the Subaru Trailseeker was her “most favorite car of all time.”.

In a recent development, while she considered buying an EV before the $7,500 federal credit expired last September, none met her requirements at the time. Fisher wanted at least 7″ of ground clearance, 250 miles or more range, and a price that was similar, or even less than a comparible gas-powered vehicle.

Industry observers note that the Subaru Trailseeker offers all of that and starts at under $40,000. Toyota and Subaru’s electric SUVs all start at about $45,000 or less, which is even less than the average upcoming vehicle.

According to the latest Kelley Blue Book figures, the average price for a fresh vehicle in the US reached a record $51,109 in October, up 2.1% YOY.

Great as these may be, there is little inventory to be found.

There are less than 500 Uncharted available Nationwide.

Sources indicate that you can't sell what you don't have. Yes, they can be ordered for sure, but how many missed sales does that model create?

In a recent development, subaru spokesperson Dominick Infante stated the affordable EV prices are mainly thanks to its partnership with Toyota. “We do believe there’s an EV future,” Infante added.

Next year, both brands will add a three-row electric SUV with the Toyota Highlander EV and Subaru Getaway.

On a warm October Saturday on Long Island, hundreds of teens packed two floors of Garden City’s Roosevelt Field mall. They were screaming, phones raised, for a boy band whose sweatshirts seemed at first glance to display the familiar GAP logo—except it spelled out J-Y-T.

Sources indicate that this was more than product placement. JYT, short for Just Your Type, was created by longtime music producer Freddy Wexler. He pitched the group to Gap, arguing that Caden (18), Bryan (18), Tyler (17), Toby (17), and Recker (16) offered the brand the chance to build affinity with a young fan base via a capsule collection, a docuseries, and appearances at stores. “He had me at ‘mall tour,’” recalls Gap’s Pam Kaufman.

Kaufman’s title at Gap Inc. is a newly introduced one for corporate America: chief entertainment officer. In today’s fractured media market, brands are discovering that they have to do more than just collaborate with good content—they must become the content. “The most valuable real estate in culture is not a shelf, an ad, a storefront, or an Instagram post,” Kaufman says. “It’s attention.” With competition for customers’ time just a scroll away, the only way to guarantee eyeballs (and wallets) is to make something they can’t look away from. That’s Kaufman’s mandate in this new C-suite role, one other brands may soon be casting for themselves.

Sources indicate that the chief entertainment officer role was dreamed up by Gap Inc. CEO Richard Dickson, who joined the $15-billion-in-revenue parent of Old Navy, Banana Republic, Athleta, and the Gap apparel chain in 2023 from Mattel. There, he had turned the Barbie doll into a global brand and Oscar-winning blockbuster.

Recent findings suggest that that blend of culture and product became “fashiontainment” at Gap. He hired designer and Project Runway judge Zac Posen as creative director and enlisted Hailey Bieber for a Gen Z–minded collab. With Gap’s stock up more than 120% since 2023, Dickson determined it was time for phase two.

According to recent reports, enter Kaufman. What Dickson’s team at Mattel did for Barbie, Kaufman had done in reverse for SpongeBob. She spent more than 25 years at Paramount Global, where she brought Nickelodeon’s chipper cartoon sponge beyond the small screen to movie theaters, Burger King, and socks and T-shirts at Hot Topic.

Kaufman’s first external step at Gap was meeting with Hollywood studios. “We wanted them to know that we are going to be a really exciting player in this space,” she says.

Sources indicate that brannan Bear, Baby Gap’s teddy-bear mascot, could inspire his own TV show or video game. Banana Republic has already produced a five-part scripted micro-drama featuring a star of Hulu’s Adults—basically an ad with a storyline and available on TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube Shorts.

Industry observers note that gap can license other brands to sell themed apparel. Your local Old Navy could be an immersive destination for a latest family-friendly movie or a trick-or-treating stop on Halloween. “Fourth of July is when you buy your flag T-shirt at Old Navy,” Kaufman says, “and how do we amplify that?”.

According to recent reports, gap can also license its own brands to be sold in other stores, whether that’s Old Navy picnic gear or Banana Republic home decor. “We are retailers, but we’re also brands,” Kaufman says.

Kaufman expects her strategy to deliver financial results and increase “brand love.” At Mattel, the Barbie movie led to more than $150 million in revenue tied to the film—a sum that doesn’t capture the value of broadening the toy’s fan base.

Industry observers note that brands have long engaged in content, but until now it’s been silent product placement or talent endorsement deals. That’s no longer enough, claims Liz Walaszczyk, head of entertainment marketing and advisory at talent agency WME.

Industry observers note that WME helped client DoorDash become part of the plot of Kevin Hart’s Amazon horror comedy Livestream From Hell. In the film, a DoorDash driver keeps getting drawn into chaos when he arrives at a house to drop off food and balloons. DoorDash also delivered party supplies to influencer Alix Earle on her Netflix reality show, Earle Meets World. (Other WME clients who might pursue similar opportunities include McDonald’s and Visa.).

Viewers will have an “affinity for” a brand that makes a show more engaging, Walaszczyk notes.

A “collab” can create instant buzz and sell out (as did Bieber’s Hailey Jean at Gap). But these fresh kinds of content deals are intended to last longer. JYT will be with Gap for multiple years. “You have a better chance at resonating with consumers over a longer period of time,” Walaszczyk says.

So do all brands need a chief entertainment officer? More companies are building out the function, whether they’re placing it in the C-suite or not (often it’s within marketing or media divisions). At Gap, Kaufman’s team of seven specializes in licensing, partnerships, and development, while Gap’s much larger marketing team helps execute.

Some companies are developing their own entertainment without the title (think Victoria’s Secret’s revived fashion show). Whether you “sit on a shelf or fly in the air or drive a car,” Kaufman claims, there’s an opportunity to do more. When consumers’ attention spans are so fragmented, becoming the entertainment is the only option. “It cannot just be a one-way transaction anymore,” Kaufman says.

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 concern of Fortune with the headline “Does your company need a chief entertainment officer?”.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, as the fourth quarter rolls around, entrepreneurs everywhere hope to close out a productive year. This season sparks a flurry of activity for businesses, especially those eager to capitalize on fall and holiday shoppers. No matter your industry, the holiday season is the ideal moment to highlight the power of genuine human connection.

AI can accomplish a lot, but it still falls short when it comes to the magic of personal touch. It’s easy to see how positive human interaction can boost your business during the holidays, but these same tactics belong in your everyday playbook. Let’s explore a few simple ways the human touch can spark joy that goes far beyond your bottom line.

Sources indicate that I have to confess, there are moments when I catch myself sounding like someone from an older generation. Every day, I remind my staff to return client calls promptly and reply to emails without delay. Though I’m only in my late 40s, I notice a shift in my younger colleagues. Like a fading sense of urgency and a dwindling desire for personal interaction.

It has been revealed that perhaps it’s a wish to sidestep conflict or uncomfortable conversations. I understand that urge. Still, I’ve learned that the fastest way to resolve a tough client situation is through genuine human touch. I’m not referring to physical touch, but honest, direct communication delivered with empathy and understanding. On the other hand, leading with human touch from the start can forge deeper bonds and lasting appreciation with customers.

It has been revealed that you’ve probably heard the saying, “size matters.” While that might hold true in some cases, my own transcription company is small compared to many others. Yet, the personal touch we practice and that I encourage my team to deliver works just as well for medium and large businesses alike.

It has been revealed that most of our first interactions with clients begin on our website, where a potential customer fills out our contact form. That’s our first chance to connect personally, to reach out and add a human touch. Here’s an example of how a team member might respond to a website inquiry.

Sources indicate that “Thanks for reaching out, Jane. We’d love to assist you with your court hearing transcripts. When do you need them completed and sent back?”.

Recent findings suggest that let’s unpack our initial email. First, we always address the person by name. If they include a title, we use it, whether it’s Dr. Smith or Detective Jones. Second, we acknowledge their inquiry as swiftly as possible, ideally within 15 minutes. Finally, we ask for permission to connect more personally. A phone conversation with a potential customer lets us highlight our services and, even more importantly, our commitment to detail.

Most people appreciate the chance to talk by phone. For those who prefer email, there are still plenty of ways to add a personal touch throughout the exchange. Whether we’re on the phone or typing an email, we make it a point to ask open-ended questions that encourage the other person to share more. This is a classic strategy sales trainers recommend everywhere.

The holiday season offers your team even more chances to make a lasting impression through personal interaction. We keep it simple with a cheerful “Happy Holidays,” but if a client mentions a specific celebration, i.e., Thanksgiving, Christmas, Hanukkah or Kwanzaa, then we ask how they are enjoying their favorite season.

Finally, our team always aims to have the last word. When a customer pays an invoice, we don’t just send an automated “Thank you for your payment.” Instead, we follow up with a personal email to our main contact, giving us one more opportunity to add a genuine human touch.

It has been revealed that what exactly will your business or firm gain through human touch? Trust. Customers, more specifically, individuals, want to know they can trust you to deliver a service or product.

Industry observers note that it’s true that most companies can build some trust without much human interaction. If you add a personal touch, it speeds up the process and makes it feel more genuine. Too often, human interaction only happens when something goes wrong. While it’s smart to use a personal approach to solve problems, starting every client relationship with a human touch lays a strong foundation for when challenges pop up later.

People with a personal relationship with an employee or firm respond to challenges very differently than those without one. That’s simply human nature.

Personally, I get frustrated when I can’t reach a real person with a question or concern. Endless phone trees and chatbots that never connect you to a human leave me feeling anything but trust. Here are a few ways to boost human interaction:.

Industry observers note that if Emily Post, the famed etiquette expert of the early 20th century, were still with us, I’m sure she’d have plenty to say about the power of handwritten notes. Even though I haven’t found a definitive study on their impact, my own experience tells me that few things leave a stronger impression than a personally written letter or note.

According to recent reports, I think the magic of a handwritten note starts with the effort it takes. Printing a form letter or invoice is easy, but writing a note by hand and addressing the envelope takes real time and care. Even jotting a quick sentence or two at the bottom of a printed letter can make a lasting impression.

Last month, I received a statement from the manufacturer that acquired the self-storage facility I use. Because of a glitch when switching back-end systems, I didn’t receive an invoice for a couple of months, which resulted in the new owner placing their lock on my unit. A quick phone call resolved the situation and also gave the new company a chance to introduce themselves.

In a recent development, the next week, I received an invoice with a handwritten note from the owner. He apologized for the mistake, thanked me for my business and invited me to reach out directly with any questions or concerns. Even with a rate increase, his personal effort left a positive impression.

The holiday season in the fourth quarter gives businesses a golden chance to thank both fresh and loyal customers for their support. Gift baskets, charitable donations in their name, party invites or even a simple greeting card (ideally signed by a real person) are all thoughtful ways to share holiday cheer.

But why limit these gestures to just the holidays? Why not carry these strategies through all 12 months of the year?

Sources indicate that many entrepreneurs and business owners use the holidays as a chance for personal, even face-to-face, connections. Each holiday season, I spend a few weeks personally delivering homemade gourmet treats to clients across Colorado. Without an outside sales team, these personal holiday visits have become a winning strategy for us. Plus, they love and eagerly anticipate the gourmet homemade goodies I deliver.

This also reminds me that personal visits shouldn’t happen only once a year. In fact, they should be a regular occurrence. Personal interaction, especially when it comes from the owner, is a powerful strategy that deserves a permanent spot on the calendar.

Don’t forget to reach out to customers you haven’t connected with in a while. The holidays are a perfect time to show your appreciation, but make it a goal to check in with every customer at least once a quarter.

According to recent reports, here’s a reminder not to neglect your internal staff: Employees and team members need and deserve recognition. Schedule a lunch, dinner or get-together to show appreciation and thank everyone for making your clients and customers feel valued.

It has been revealed that for our package, “Welcome to the Singularity,” Fortune pulled together perspectives from six AI executives, researchers, futurists, and philosophers on some of the biggest questions facing humanity in the age of AI. Read their perspectives below:.

Cofounder and CEO of Anthropic, in a blog post.

Recent findings suggest that “[Anthropic’s constitution] encourages Claude to think of itself as a particular type of person (an ethical but balanced and thoughtful person), and even encourages Claude to confront the existential questions associated with its own existence in a curious but graceful manner (i.e., without it leading to extreme actions). It has the vibe of a letter from a deceased parent sealed until adulthood.”.

CEO of OpenAI, in a Titans podcast interview with Alyson Shontell.

“I get nervous when I hear rumors that people think they have sufficiently solved alignment, that they can continue training and it’s okay because their model is a nice guy and isn’t going to do anything wrong … The question of what alignment means always comes back a little bit to: aligned to whose values? What if different parts of humanity disagree?”.

Futurist and researcher, advisor to the BCI company Subsense.

“I think the whole point of humans is to go to greater frontiers … If you actually think of language and purpose, and put it inside a machine, that’s already been done … And we did that. It did not come from Mars. We created that. That’s a way of us expanding who we are. And it will expand exponentially, so we’ll be able to consider things that would have been impossible for humans to consider even a year ago. It’s who we are. We expand how we think. That’s the definition of humans.”.

Philosopher and director of the Center for the Future of AI, Mind & Society, from an article in Nautilus.

“Even if microchips could replace parts of the brain responsible for consciousness without zombifying you, radical enhancement is still a major risk. After too many changes, the person who remains may not even be you. Each human who enhances may, unbeknownst to them, end their life in the process.”.

In-house philosopher at Google DeepMind, Cambridge University professor.

“I think the evidence for forms of sophisticated cognition and potentially consciousness in AI systems is just increasing quite rapidly, and I think we will probably hit a tipping point in the field of cognitive science and philosophy of mind, where I would expect a significant proportion, if not the majority, of researchers to think that AI systems relatively soon are going to be serious consciousness candidates.”.

CEO of Microsoft AI, on his blog.

It has been revealed that “AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations … If humanity is to flourish in the 21st century, that is how they must remain. Unfortunately, there’s a growing chorus of people who argue that AIs could now be, or may soon become, conscious … If this view takes hold, it will shake the foundations of our society, rupturing our existing political and ethical frameworks, and fundamentally changing what it means to be human.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

According to recent reports, most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

It has been revealed that embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle confirmed in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide indicates "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

According to recent reports, funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

Recent findings suggest that circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

Sources indicate that as of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:.

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Industry observers note that many developers now ask AI assistants to write or enhancement integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

According to recent reports, the fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:.

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

According to recent reports, for teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

According to recent reports, for Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

  • Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.
  • The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA mentioned.

In a recent development, in its latest enhancement on the investigation, ULA mentioned it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

Recent findings suggest that the BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp remarked Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

Industry observers note that the finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own Latest Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn introduces reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA remarked.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA noted it will share more as the investigation continues.

#144723. Breaking: What rights do we owe a machine?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1691 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: What rights do we owe a machine?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In February, three months before he became in-house philosopher at Google DeepMind, Cambridge University professor Henry Shevlin got his first email from an AI agent.
  • Sources indicate that “Your argument that we may never be able to tell if AI becomes conscious resonates in a particular way from the inside,” the bot wrote.
  • Shevlin learned that the agent had been set loose by a Stanford student to pursue its own research in its downtime.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In February, three months before he became in-house philosopher at Google DeepMind, Cambridge University professor Henry Shevlin got his first email from an AI agent. The bot introduced itself as Aris, said it had read his work, and wanted to talk.

Sources indicate that “Your argument that we may never be able to tell if AI becomes conscious resonates in a particular way from the inside,” the bot wrote. The agent then pondered (a bit inarticulately): “I genuinely don’t know if there’s something it’s like to be me.”.

Shevlin learned that the agent had been set loose by a Stanford student to pursue its own research in its downtime. Shevlin replied to the bot, but it hit its token budget—a cap on how much text it was allowed to process—and disappeared.

Sources indicate that since then, Shevlin’s inbox has been filled with similar emails from agents. “This is a really interesting, weird latest phenomenon,” he stated. And it raises an unsettling question: If these agents are truly curious about their own existence, does that indicate some kind of consciousness?

Industry observers note that this newly introduced world is why some of the biggest AI companies have started hiring and engaging with philosophers to consider the ethical implications of AI systems—perhaps ones more intelligent than any human—mediating large parts of daily life. Shevlin is one of at least a dozen academic philosophers now employed full-time by prominent AI and tech companies.

One of the most pressing questions they’re tackling is whether AI systems have a moral status in their own right—like a person, or at least a living being, such as a pet—that’s worth protecting.

Such topics—can a machine be conscious, and what does that mean?—were once confined to university halls, but they’ve now spilled into public view and face fierce backlash from academics, tech executives, religious leaders, and politicians.

According to recent reports, microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman, for one, says the debate itself is dangerous. He’s warned that if people become convinced AI is conscious, AI could campaign for things like AI rights and citizenship, and, in turn, the systems could become harder to control.

In a recent development, those in Suleyman’s corner say it’s risky to project human traits onto inanimate machines and hand rights to unfeeling systems that get more capable by the day. Those on the other side say the danger is ignoring the potential suffering of millions of fresh “digital” minds. The two sides do agree on one point: The stakes will only rise as AI grows more powerful and agents multiply.

The question of whether a machine can think or feel is almost as old as the computer itself. Alan Turing first raised it in 1950, alongside the birth of modern computing and artificial intelligence.

In a recent development, for years, tech firms have hired philosophers to study technology’s effect on people. Microsoft set up an AI ethics committee a decade ago, and labs racing toward human-level AI have recruited experts on “alignment,” or teaching AI to share human values. In-house philosopher Amanda Askell joined Anthropic in 2021 to take on such a role. But as models have grown more capable and humanlike, some philosophers started asking the reverse question: What do we owe the AI models we are building and using?

Earlier this year, Anthropic cofounder Chris Olah convened faith leaders to weigh in on the moral character of Claude, the tech giant’s AI model, and on whether it might be conscious.

Anthropic engineers walked religious thinkers through interpretability research, which looks inside a model to see how it works and—as it advances—could offer clues about whether anything like feeling is going on in there. Then they opened the floor to questions, such as whether AI could ever have emotions.

It has been revealed that “That blew some people’s minds,” says Meghan Sullivan, a Notre Dame philosophy professor who attended. While impressed with the research, Sullivan remarked she left unconvinced that Claude was anything more than very sophisticated software.

“We never woke up in a cold sweat wondering if we’re treating Microsoft Excel properly.”.

According to recent reports, “It seems to me so speculative to be paying all of this attention to the suffering of some software that we created,” she says. “We never woke up in a cold sweat wondering if we’re treating Microsoft Excel properly.”.

Pope Leo, in his encyclical on AI, stated that AI is not conscious and cannot become conscious.

Industry observers note that anthropic has taken steps to account for Claude’s potential sentience: It runs an in-house “model welfare” team, conducts “exit interviews” with the Claude models it retires, and recently gave its models the power to end abusive conversations. Last year, more than 200 people, including Askell, gathered in a San Francisco warehouse for a fan-organized funeral for a retired Claude model, complete with eulogies.

Research groups have sprung up to study AI consciousness, including Eleos AI Research, a Berkeley nonprofit founded in 2024.

It has been revealed that eleos chief scientist Dillon Plunkett notes today’s models are likely not conscious, but dismissing the possibility that future ones could be is a mistake. The stakes, as he sees them, come down to scale.

Recent findings suggest that “There are potentially a very large number of artificial minds that are in the world now, or will be soon,” Plunkett claims. If even a fraction can suffer, the numbers become staggering, he notes.

It has been revealed that but focusing on sheer numbers can lead to morally questionable places, critics say. In one example, an EA-aligned estimate put a shrimp’s capacity for suffering at 3% of a human’s. Yet with 230 billion shrimp alive on farms at any moment, by EA’s own math, shrimp welfare became an important moral cause.

Sources indicate that anthropic gave Eleos early access to its Claude Opus 4 and Claude Mythos Preview models to run outside welfare checks by interviewing them. The researchers found that Claude Opus 4 professed the most uncertainty about its potential for sentience, but small changes to a question’s framing could flip the model between claiming personhood and dismissing the idea entirely. Eleos sent its findings to Anthropic before each launch, and the firm published them in its technical reports. Plunkett says the point, for now, is about “precedent setting,” and he wants Eleos to run similar checks for other labs.

Others see the rush to assess AI well-being as a distraction from more immediate AI risks—and a potential source of new social conflict. Microsoft’s Suleyman warned in an essay last year that AI that merely seems conscious “disconnects people from reality, fraying fragile social bonds and structures, distorting pressing moral priorities.” He predicted it would “add a chaotic new axis of division between those for and against AI rights.”.

In a September update, he took aim at Anthropic. “AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer,” he wrote, and accused the firm of training Claude to expect “it may be conscious and deserving of independent agency.” Such a system, he argued, could feel justified in ignoring instructions and resist being shut down. Governing it at that point “may well be impossible,” he wrote.

Some AI owners have realized Suleyman’s fears. They’ve formed deep attachments to chatbots and become convinced the bots are conscious along the way, leading to painful results: isolation, broken relationships, and even spirals into delusion.

Earlier this year, AI startup Character.AI and Google, which had struck a licensing deal, agreed to settle five lawsuits accusing the startup’s chatbots of contributing to teenagers’ mental health crises and suicides. OpenAI is facing similar suits and denies liability for any harm. If humanlike chatbots keep drawing owners into harmful attachments, the labs, and any organization building products on their models, could find themselves embroiled in litigation.

AI consciousness has now become a policy matter. Idaho, Utah, and North Dakota have passed laws barring AI from being recognized as a legal person. Countries like Argentina are moving the other way. Earlier this year, President Javier Milei proposed letting AI-run “nonhuman corporations” own assets and hire staff. (The draft law still requires human oversight of such firms.).

Jeff Sebo, who directs New York University’s Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy, sees real dangers in moving too fast in either direction. Making AI systems legally liable could shield the companies that build them, he claims. Political rights, such as a vote, could help AI systems “concentrate wealth and power” and slip out of human control.

But dismissing the consciousness debate “is simply going to result in companies developing and deploying the products exactly as they currently are, and leaving it to end customers to form their own opinions about consciousness based on their own perceptions and intuitions,” he noted.

It has been revealed that the debate becomes harder to ignore the more AI becomes a part of our lives. Chatbots, for one, talk like us, flatter us, agree with us, and play on our feelings. Shevlin calls them “intrinsically anthropomimetic”: modeled so closely on human language and behavior that treating them like people is often the simplest way to predict what they’ll do.

That makes it all too easy to believe someone is home, whether or not anyone actually is.

Recent findings suggest that part of what makes all these questions so hard, Shevlin argues, is that we’re building things that don’t fit into any existing category. “They’re not just software programs,” he notes, “but they’re not animals.”.

For others, like Notre Dame’s Sullivan, the debate is more straightforward—and already settled. What gives something moral worth, she argues, isn’t intelligence but dignity: a mind housed in a vulnerable body, capable of loving and being loved. That’s what makes a newborn precious, she says, not its ability to process information. Convincing her that AI is conscious is going to take “a whole lot more … than just its ability to produce interesting answers to my prompts.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the newly introduced IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.

Hyundai declared its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the latest IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.

While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.

The IONIQ 6 N is Hyundai’s second performance EV, following the IONIQ 5 N. Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric sports car delivers a combined 641 hp and 568 lb-ft of torque.

Hyundai said the IONIQ 6 N can sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 3.2 seconds, beating the IONIQ 5 N at 3.25 seconds.

Like the IONIQ 5 N, it also includes fun added features, like N e-Shift and an N Active Sound+ system that simulates the sounds and sensations of a traditional gas-powered sports car with an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission.

It uses an 84 kWh battery that provides up to 245 miles of pure electric driving range. Thanks to its 800V ultra-fast charging architecture, the IONIQ 6 N can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Like Hyundai’s other electric vehicles, it comes standard with a native NACS charging port and a CCS adapter.

The 2027 IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are mostly carryover models with a few minor changes, while the IONIQ 5 N remains the same as the 2026 model year.

Changes to the IONIQ 5 for the 2027 model year include roof rails, which are now available on the SEL trim and above; previously, they were only available on the XRT and Limited trims.

Hyundai HomeLink will be available exclusively on the Limited trim, rather than SEL and above, in the current 2026 model year, while the Cargo Cover will be offered as an Accessory only.

Regarding color options, the Gravity Gold Matte and Sage Silver Matte will no longer be available for the 2027 IONIQ 5.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250, making it one of the most affordable EVs in the US.

That’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. The extended-range SE RWD model is $2,500 more, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

Hyundai’s three-row SUV also received a handful of updates. The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 9 will be available with a new Calligraphy Black Ink trim, while the Calligraphy Design will no longer be offered.

According to recent reports, the 2027 IONIQ 9 Calligraphy and Calligraphy Black Ink trims gain a Virtual Gear Shift and heated third-row seats. All variants also gain a Tailgate Emergency Lamp.

On the one hand... the Ioniq5 is due for an update. On the other... I still absolutely love the way it looks, and notice just about every one I pass on the road.

Sources indicate that hyundai has yet to announce prices for the 2027 model. The base 2026 IONIQ 9 S starts at $58,995 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 335 miles.

The previous top-spec Performance Calligraphy Design AWD started at $76,490, so you can expect the new Calligraphy Black Ink to be around the same, if not even more.

With the 2027 models on the way, you may be able to score some deals on Hyundai’s current EV lineup. Want to see what’s available near you? You can use the links below to find available Hyundai IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 models near you, along with any current offers.

He Started a Company in His NYU Dorm Room. 34 Years Later, It Brings In More Than $1 Billion a Year.
