⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At age 23, Phil Shawe was pursuing an MBA at NYU when he had a business idea that made some people around him skeptical.
  • In a recent development, shawe saw an opening.
  • Recent findings suggest that “I met my former partner in business school, and she had worked at the largest translation tech giant at the time, Berlitz,” Shawe says in a new interview with Entrepreneur.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At age 23, Phil Shawe was pursuing an MBA at NYU when he had a business idea that made some people around him skeptical. Why spend money on business school, thousands of dollars, only to start a small translation tech giant?

In a recent development, shawe saw an opening. Advertising agencies, law firms and big corporations needed language services. He believed he could deliver something better than what was currently on the market.

Recent findings suggest that “I met my former partner in business school, and she had worked at the largest translation tech giant at the time, Berlitz,” Shawe says in a new interview with Entrepreneur. “She worked there in New York, and they were constantly unable to satisfy clients. We theorized that there was a better mousetrap to build in the language business.”.

Recent findings suggest that in 1992, Shawe and his business partner, Liz Elting, co-founded TransPerfect from his NYU dorm room. They didn’t have a large financial backer underwriting their ambitions. They financed the business themselves, leaned on credit cards and tried to find customers.

First, the founders had to persuade someone to hire them.

“We would basically cold-call till our fingers bled,” Shawe indicates.

They also faxed prospects and sent mailers containing information and brochures. As projects came in, they built a network of linguists to handle the work. Shawe’s description of the early sales strategy is simple: “Brute force clients in the door.”.

Recent findings suggest that shawe has since helped turn that operation into a business generating $1.32 billion in annual revenue. He notes that TransPerfect now has more than 10,000 employees, whose work extends from translating contracts and supporting global drug studies to developing software and helping companies implement AI.

Shawe notes that about half of the firm’s revenue still comes from language translation services. The rest comes from technology consulting and other businesses shaped around customer needs.

According to recent reports, as TransPerfect has grown, so has Shawe’s net worth. According to the Forbes billionaires list, Shawe, 57, is currently worth $1.7 billion.

It has been revealed that transPerfect produced about $400,000 in revenue in its first year, Shawe says. He recalls that the organization broke even that year, with little choice but to keep spending below what it brought in.

The founders reinvested in the firm as it grew. There was an exception to the largely self-financed approach: In 1998, Shawe notes, they separated the technology business from the traditional translation operation and raised $4.1 million, with Deutsche Bank as the lead investor.

After the internet bubble burst, he and his partner used their own money to return investors’ original capital. Shawe later bought out his partner in 2018.

Shawe does not credit the organization’s rise entirely to persistence. TransPerfect arrived as the internet and globalization created upcoming connections across borders. The founders worked hard, but the timing helped.

However, as the organization expanded, landing work was not the toughest problem. Shawe says hiring and retaining people who could deliver the work became harder. The founders could not oversee every project or client relationship, so training employees became increasingly important.

Growth also taught Shawe a costly lesson about the difference between a customer’s promise and a binding commitment.

Sources indicate that early on, a client indicated that a substantial amount of business was coming. TransPerfect opened an Atlanta office, placed people on-site and made significant investments to prepare. Then the customer changed course, leaving the company financially exposed.

“It almost put us out of business,” Shawe indicates.

He says that situation was his most expensive mistake as a founder. The error was investing heavily in a venture without adequate contractual protection. His takeaway was not to make massive capital commitments for business that a customer has only verbally agreed to provide.

According to recent reports, transPerfect started with cold outreach. Keeping customers helped it scale. “If you want a business to grow, the most important thing you can do is retain your customers,” Shawe says.

According to recent reports, for TransPerfect, that meant hitting deadlines and delivering projects in the formats clients expect. Consistently performing well could turn a customer contact into an internal advocate, or someone willing to recommend the manufacturer to another team or division.

Shawe says referrals between divisions of large corporations is an important source of business. TransPerfect prefers to obtain latest customers through recommendations from within an organization, and much of its sales activity now involves expanding services for existing customers.

TransPerfect also organized around industries. Once it had enough banking work, for example, it could build a dedicated finance division staffed with people who understood that sector. It applied the same approach to law firms, life sciences and luxury brands.

The company’s goal is to become a trusted advisor, not simply a supplier accepting translation orders. Listening to customers opened doors. For example, legal translation clients needed help with electronic discovery, or finding and processing digital information for litigation. TransPerfect expanded into those services, and Shawe claims the e-discovery and litigation-support business is on pace to generate $160 million or more this year.

“E-discovery and litigation support is not something that we started in the dorm room, but over the years enough of our customers communicated to us that they needed better or different services in this field, and that’s what drew us into it,” Shawe notes.

He added that the business is now a “huge contributor” to the company’s annual revenue.

TransPerfect faces newly introduced advancements like AI and rapid translation features from tech giants like Apple and Google. Shawe says that TransPerfect must bring new technology to customers.

“We want to be the ones constantly disrupting our own business,” he indicates.

Sources indicate that shawe has witnessed several waves of technology reshape translation, including neural machine translation, or AI that automatically translates text with advanced technology, and now large language models, or AI programs trained on massive amounts of text data. Shawe states each change has created ways to accomplish more with fewer resources.

He notes that if formatting a multilingual manual once required 40 hours, and software can reduce that work to an hour or 15 minutes, TransPerfect should introduce the software, even if it loses billable hours.

“It might decrease our revenue in the short term, but it’s going to cement our client relationship and allow us to grow the business with that customer in the long term,” Shawe says.

According to recent reports, transPerfect can go beyond translating words and help businesses use language technology effectively. Shawe notes customers continue to turn to the organization for additional languages and higher-risk content even as automation handles more work.

He advises young founders to “raise as little money as possible” and “show real revenues as much as you can.”.

If he were starting from scratch with limited money and no network, he says he would focus on building relationships with customers and team members.

“These contacts that you make when you’re young, they compound like interest, and the value of those relationships also compounds,” Shawe says.

“I met my former partner in business school, and she had worked at the largest translation organization at the time, Berlitz,” Shawe notes in a new interview with Entrepreneur. “She worked there in New York, and they were constantly unable to satisfy clients. We theorized that there was a better mousetrap to build in the language business.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The XRP ETF market might be bracing to close a record-breaking month of outflows as demand for the XRP-based investment product has remained on hold all through the month.

This comes as the prolonged and intense market volatility has extended to the ETF ecosystem, causing institutional investors to withdraw their capital.

With November just about three weeks gone, the latest data from SoSoValue shows that XRP ETFs have already recorded a total of $30.76 million in net outflows this November.

Previous ETF data indicates that March remains the only month in which spot XRP ETFs have recorded net outflows since their launch.

While it still stands as the record outflow month for XRP ETFs, investors withdrew about $31.16 million from the funds during that month.

This means that the persistent withdrawals seen this month have brought the November outflow dangerously close to its previous monthly record seen in March.

Apparently, the spot XRP ETFs are on track to close November as their worst-performing month since launch, with just about $1 million left to hit the record.

Further data also shows that the spot XRP ETFs have yet to record a single day of net inflows throughout November, as the persistent price decline has caused investors to slow down their purchases.

As such, the influx of fresh capital into the spot XRP ETF market has remained on hold amid growing market uncertainty and a shift in investor sentiment.

‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.
  • The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

Sources indicate that sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

According to recent reports, she’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Sources indicate that paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” Fresh America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

In a recent development, sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers stated they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

It has been revealed that in its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates mentioned she welcomed the conversation.

According to recent reports, “I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

Recent findings suggest that the summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

In a recent development, proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration proposal and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:.

According to recent reports, it also indicates plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain.".

In a recent development, A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis.".

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":.

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Sources indicate that mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

Industry observers note that the tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

Industry observers note that the portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks.".

Sources indicate that why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

Recent findings suggest that at launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

According to recent reports, proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

According to recent reports, so Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

It has been revealed that for now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:.

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":.

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

#144714. Want to Write Your First Novel? Here Are 10 Books to Read Before Picking Up Your Pen.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1711 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

Want to Write Your First Novel? Here Are 10 Books to Read Before Picking Up Your Pen.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that you have an idea for a fiction novel that you can’t stop thinking about.
  • So you open a blank document, type a sentence, pause for a moment, then delete it.
  • Before you try to answer every question on your own, turn to your bookshelf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that you have an idea for a fiction novel that you can’t stop thinking about. Maybe it’s a character, a setting or a scene you’ve played out in your head countless times. No matter what it is, you want to explore this latest world.

So you open a blank document, type a sentence, pause for a moment, then delete it. Faced with an empty page, you wonder how your seed of an idea is supposed to become an entire book. How can a formless thought take shape?

Before you try to answer every question on your own, turn to your bookshelf. Learn the craft of writing from people who have done it before you. How does a writer make you care about a stranger, a made-up character, within the first few lines? What keeps you reading when little seems to happen?

Recent findings suggest that then there’s the ending. How does an ending feel both surprising and inevitable?

Sources indicate that the following 10 books offer a place to explore those questions. Some explain how to build a plot or develop a character. Others help you manage doubt and pay attention. They all treat fiction as a craft you can study. They can also keep you organization as you begin writing a story of your own and remind you that you are not alone in your pursuit of writing a novel.

On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft.

Author Stephen King has published over 60 novels and sold more than 350 million copies of his books globally. In this book, he combines his personal story of becoming a writer with a practical account of how he works. In the autobiographical sections, he reveals his early encounters with storytelling, his struggles before getting published for the first time and how writing fits into the rest of his life. He also explores the practical aspects of writing, including vocabulary, grammar, description, dialogue and revision. His approach is direct and conversational. The book also features a marked-up manuscript that demonstrates actual revisions, which can be helpful for writers thinking about the process of editing. Overall, King offers encouragement and technical advice for first-time novelists.

Bird by Bird: Some Instructions on Writing and Life.

According to recent reports, anne Lamott starts this book with a family story. Her brother left a report about birds until the last minute and felt overwhelmed by everything he had to do. Their father told him to take it bird by bird, inspiring the title of the book. That small instruction becomes the book’s central approach to writing. Instead of confronting the project as an impossible whole, attend to one manageable piece at a time. Lamott applies that approach to rough drafts and the emotional confusion of creative work. She offers humor and permission to produce messy drafts. Her advice is to reduce the task into bite-sized parts, accept imperfection and continue even when there is no guarantee of a future reward.

Writing Down the Bones: Freeing the Writer Within.

In this book, popular author Natalie Goldberg approaches writing as a practice strengthened through repetition. She offers short reflections and exercises that help writers get words onto the page before their inner judgment shuts them down. The exercises provide a low-pressure space for discovering memories, images and even unexpected connections. The focus is on developing an open relationship with the act of writing. Goldberg pushes writers to keep the hand moving and resist the urge to cross out thoughts immediately. These small habits help the writer notice more and censor less when creating material. If you spend more time evaluating possible sentences rather than writing them, this is the book for you. It has sold more than one million copies.

Story Genius: How to Use Brain Science to Go Beyond Outlining and Write a Riveting Novel (Before You Waste Three Years Writing 327 Pages That Go Nowhere).

Recent findings suggest that author Lisa Cron is a story coach, speaker and author who has previously worked as a literary agent. She asks writers to look beneath the surface events of a story. In other words, an unusual situation or dramatic accident is not enough by itself. What matters is how that event affects a particular person, given that person’s unique worldview. Her method places the protagonist’s internal struggle at the center of the novel’s development. The book moves from an initial idea to a developed blueprint, including scenes. Its aim is to connect incidents through a protagonist’s changing interiority. Read this when you know what happens in your novel but cannot explain why it matters to the main character living through it.

Save the Cat! Writes a Novel: The Last Book On Novel Writing You’ll Ever Need.

Sources indicate that jessica Brody is the bestselling author of more than 20 novels, mainly young adult fiction. This book organizes story structure around 15 major developments, extending from the opening image to the finale. It also introduces 10 story categories based on patterns of conflict and transformation, giving writers ways to understand the kind of narrative they are building. The appeal is clarity. The writer can examine the purpose of different turning points in their novel. What debuts the central journey? When does the situation change? How does the ending express what the protagonist has learned? Read this if your first novel feels exciting in fragments but isn’t coming together as a whole.

Plot & Structure (Write Great Fiction).

Former trial lawyer James Scott Bell offers a practical guide to creating a plot and understanding how its parts fit together. He addresses the relationship between plot and structure and the differences between commercial and literary fiction. The emphasis is on usable techniques. Bell’s central framework is called LOCK, which stands for lead, objective, confrontation and knockout. These elements direct attention toward a compelling central character, a clear goal, meaningful opposition and a strong ending. Using these attributes, you can decide if a story has enough pressure and direction to sustain the reader’s interest. What is your protagonist trying to achieve? What prevents success? What would make the resolution satisfying?

Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story.

Recent findings suggest that author Ursula K. Le Guin turns her attention to the language by which a story reaches the reader. Her writing guide combines discussion with exercises. She walks readers through drills in storytelling, point of view and grammar. The exercises make this a book to use actively. Le Guin notes that the work of a sentence is to carry the reader to the next one. She addresses how to handle exposition, or how to incorporate information into a story instead of allowing explanation to bring it to a halt. Her approach connects elements sometimes treated separately, like language and pacing. The value of this book is helping readers hear and inspect their prose. A promising plot still needs solid sentences that keep the story moving.

This style manual was privately printed in 1918 for Cornell University students by English professor William Strunk Jr., then published more widely by Harcourt in 1920. Strunk’s former student and author E. B. White revised and expanded the volume in 1959. This book concentrates on constructing clear prose. It is short, about 100 pages, which means it is perfect to consult regularly as you write. Its usefulness lies in directing a writer’s attention toward language. A novelist might be absorbed in a character’s choices while giving too little thought to how to clearly communicate those behaviors in a sentence. Strunk and White set the stage for authors to learn the conventions of clear prose. They provide a foundation from which to make deliberate stylistic choices that enhance a reader’s experience.

The Writing Life: The Classic Essay Collection on the Creative Process.

Sources indicate that annie Dillard, a Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist with experience writing fiction and nonfiction, published poetry, essays, prose and literary criticism. In The Writing Life, she offers a reflection on creative writing, not a step-by-step manual. She considers the difficulty and uncertainty of the writing process. A line of words can lead a writer into unfamiliar territory, but they may not know where to go next. What first appears promising might actually be a dead end, while a seemingly incidental encounter might become the real subject. Dillard preserves a place for the parts of writing that remain difficult, even when the writer is attentive and experienced. She offers perspective on the patience and seriousness of writing.

Refuse to Be Done: How to Write and Rewrite a Novel in Three Drafts.

Industry observers note that writer and teacher Matt Bell treats revision as a central part of novel writing. His guide divides the process into three broad stages, giving each step a different purpose. The first move helps writers generate material and move through the initial draft. The second focuses on reworking the narrative through outlining, modeling and rewriting. The third step turns toward a layered polishing process. This final stage breaks revision into specific operations, deconstructing a large and potentially overwhelming task into a series of more manageable actions. This book is worth reading before writing the first page. It offers a practical guide to making a manuscript stronger.

You have an idea for a fiction novel that you can’t stop thinking about. Maybe it’s a character, a setting or a scene you’ve played out in your head countless times. No matter what it is, you want to explore this latest world.

So you open a blank document, type a sentence, pause for a moment, then delete it. Faced with an empty page, you wonder how your seed of an idea is supposed to become an entire book. How can a formless thought take shape?

Before you try to answer every question on your own, turn to your bookshelf. Learn the craft of writing from people who have done it before you. How does a writer make you care about a stranger, a made-up character, within the first few lines? What keeps you reading when little seems to happen?

#144713. Inside the race to put computers in the human brain

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2071 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Inside the race to put computers in the human brain

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A robotic arm drills a circle into the patient’s skull, then places a quarter-size device onto the brain tissue.
  • That’s the promise of the N1 implant made by Neuralink, the brain-computer interface (BCI) company owned by Elon Musk.
  • Recent findings suggest that although no brain implants are on the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A robotic arm drills a circle into the patient’s skull, then places a quarter-size device onto the brain tissue. Dangling from it are 64 wires, each thinner than a human hair. Electrodes along the wires pick up electrical signals from neurons in the brain, and the implant transmits that data to a phone or tablet. The patient can text friends, post on social media, and even play video games—all without lifting a finger.

That’s the promise of the N1 implant made by Neuralink, the brain-computer interface (BCI) company owned by Elon Musk. Neuralink has made science fiction a reality for the approximately 26 people using the device today in the product’s testing phase. All have severe disabilities, but Musk founded the company in 2016 with the goal of far broader adoption. In 2017 he argued that humans will need to connect our brains to technology to keep up with artificial intelligence and avoid “being left behind and being effectively useless, or like a pet.” By 2025, Neuralink was valued at roughly $9.7 billion.

Recent findings suggest that although no brain implants are on the U.S. market yet, the first one that becomes available will be a watershed moment—for the tech sector, for society, arguably for humanity—setting off what those in the industry expect to be a decades-long process to merge our minds with machines. BCIs stand to become increasingly interwoven in our everyday lives, spawning new businesses and demanding new norms to govern their use.

In a recent development, at stake for the companies pioneering these devices is a potentially massive market, both for the devices and the vast troves of data they’ll gather. For the rest of us, the question is what, if anything, we gain by giving corporations access to the sanctity of our thoughts—to profit off and perhaps even shape.

In a recent development, “What you’re thinking and feeling is your last space of true privacy. It’s the most fundamental aspect of what it means to be human,” says Nita Farahany, a professor at Duke University who authored a book on defending the freedom of thought in an era of brain implants. “We are rapidly heading toward a world of brain transparency, in which scientists, doctors, governments, and companies may peer into our brains and minds at will. Companies [could] know what products we want before we do.”.

Industry observers note that neuralink is one in a growing field of U.S. companies developing BCIs, each sprinting to win Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for public sale. Those include Paradromics, which is focused on restoring speech, and Precision Neuroscience, which is pursuing a brain interface for patients with paralysis.

“It is definitely a race,” claims Chad Bouton, CEO of the BCI company Neuvotion, which makes a commercially available, AI-guided wearable that can help restore movement in stroke and spinal cord injury patients. “I think in the next three or four years we might see an FDA clearance.”.

Neuralink, with $1.3 billion in funding, more than double the next-best-funded brain implant tech giant, might seem a shoo-in to come out ahead, but a rival BCI company, called Synchron, is neck and neck in the FDA process. Synchron’s device—which is less invasive and doesn’t require a skull-breaking craniotomy—may well be first to market.

Sources indicate that thomas Oxley, founder and CEO of Synchron, revealed to Fortune that his company has implanted its Stentrode device in 15 people, adding five more since last year. In that same period, Neuralink has gone from seven patients to 26. “They’re going fast,” mentioned Oxley, who is himself a neurosurgeon.

It has been revealed that the race had been underway for years before AI became a household term with the debut of ChatGPT in 2022. But rapidly advancing AI stands to dramatically enhance the power of brain implants by allowing them to better decipher our thoughts and intentions.

Sources indicate that one day, AI-enhanced BCIs could enable us to control humanoid robots or AI agents on our behalf, taking instructions directly from our thoughts, notes Matt Angle, CEO of Paradromics. As the research goes “cognitively upstream from language,” he says, the implants could know our desires before we are even aware of them. If a human is hungry, for example, “then the BCI would already understand what we are hungry for, and it would deduce the next reasonable thing,” Angle said—perhaps ordering food on a delivery app. “It won’t be mainstream right away,” he explained, but “it’ll come sooner than a lot of people are expecting.”.

For workers, brain implants could usher in a new wave of employee surveillance in the name of productivity. Connecting a BCI to a work computer could help us type and navigate our computers faster, while also recording biological signals that reveal whether we are focused on work, or letting our minds wander. Employers could even nudge us back to work if BCIs develop two-way communication, Farahany writes in her book. She suspects punitive brain surveillance is unlikely to be tolerated by the public—but even today we accept new forms of workplace tracking, from how many times a day we badge-in to the office to transcriptions of what we say in meetings and monitoring of which applications we open on our computer.

“What you’re thinking and feeling is your last space of true privacy.”.

Some argue that the “cyborgization” of humanity has already begun, even if the devices and algorithms that we’re joined with are external to the body. In a 2017 blog post titled “The Merge,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote, “Our phones control us and tell us what to do and when; social media feeds determine how we feel; search engines decide what we think.” By 2025, an OpenAI analysis of 1.5 million ChatGPT conversations found that roughly three-quarters concerned practical guidance, information seeking, or writing—suggesting that people are increasingly turning to AI to help decide what to do and what to say.

Recent findings suggest that altman cofounded the BCI company Merge Labs in 2025, and in early 2026, OpenAI invested in it. The company’s goal is to create a more “seamless” relationship with AI—presumably ChatGPT, or one of the models behind it. A Merge Labs spokesperson wasn’t ready to reveal its product yet in our conversation, but expects to have more to share in “a couple months.”.

The portal to this latest world will open when the FDA approves the first brain implant. Getting there is a long road for aspirants: Companies in the running must go through various stages, beginning with animal testing. Once they clear that hurdle, companies can perform their first human implant and begin what’s called “early feasibility studies.”.

Recent findings suggest that then comes the pivotal study. Companies that reach this stage can expand to more patients, while also focusing on manufacturing. That means having the “whole manufacturing line established and frozen, [and] that’s a huge investment,” Oxley noted.

It also means experimentation is largely over—device design is locked, and the final trials will assess the benefits for a specific, target user. The pivotal study concludes with FDA approval to sell the products to patients with eligible, clearly defined medical conditions, with insurance likely helping to cover the cost.

Industry observers note that in 20 years, the BCI capabilities of today will likely seem rudimentary. But the technology is already capable of incredible things—no less than modern magic.

Neuralink’s first patient, Noland Arbaugh, who became paralyzed after a diving accident, has used the implant he had installed in January 2024 to play video games such as Civilization and is now working on a book in partnership with a writer.

His implant has enabled him to travel the world for speaking engagements and facilitated being in a relationship. Even though “being paralyzed still sucks,” he posted a few months ago, he’s “constantly blown away” by the advances of his implant. When I interviewed Arbaugh in 2025, he told me, “It has absolutely changed my outlook on life and what I’m able to accomplish and what I think I can do in the future. So it has given me a lot of hope for myself.”.

Synchron patients can also manipulate a computer, and the company was the first to integrate with Apple’s newly created standardized, Bluetooth-powered BCI connection in 2025. But Synchron’s device, the Stentrode, is less powerful than Neuralink’s. That’s a downside of its being significantly less invasive, perhaps making it more palatable to patients who aren’t interested in the skull-drilling that Neuralink’s N1 requires.

In a recent development, the Stentrode takes just a two-hour surgery to insert into a blood vessel near the brain, via a catheter, like a heart stent (hence the name). The sensor transmits electrical brain signals via a thin wire that tunnels under the skin to a coin-size “receiver,” embedded in the chest near the collarbone.

Synchron patients activate their implants by thinking about a part of the body, such as “Move my foot,” which an algorithm interprets as code for “Press select”—a less direct command than Neuralink’s, though miraculous in its own right.

It has been revealed that synchron, valued at nearly $1 billion in its latest funding round, is also cooking up a more powerful device, a major product launch Oxley states is coming “soon,” with a more explicit eye toward mass-market adoption. It will access more parts of the brain, not just one spot, like the Stentrode or Neuralink N1, and won’t require a craniotomy, Oxley said.

“Everyone in the field agrees that the holy grail of BCI is whole-brain sensing,” he remarked, explaining that the device could help patients with aging-related cognitive decline or dementia, behaving like a “cognitive copilot … I think that could be huge.” He framed it as a natural extension of the way today’s technology already helps us remember birthdays, auto-completes sentences in emails, or, using LLMs, writes presentations or understands our emotions.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Neuralink is experimenting with less invasive techniques. In June 2026, Neuralink unveiled it had performed its first procedure without breaking a protective layer of the brain called the dura. This is a “substantial step,” indicates Adam Marblestone, cofounder of Convergent Research, an incubator for technical startups focused on the public good, and a former scientist at Google DeepMind. “I think that’s a kind of technical tour de force, and it probably leads to a very powerful system.”.

Recent findings suggest that as much as Neuralink and Synchron are competing against each other and other U.S. companies, they face perhaps even stiffer competition from China, where the world’s first commercially available BCI was approved in March. The industry there is “very fast, very active, and very dynamic,” Oxley noted. When I asked if China’s rapid trajectory makes him nervous, he replied simply, “Yes.”.

It has been revealed that BCIs could introduce the same type of supply-chain risks as other tech that the U.S. grapples with China over—semiconductors, AI models, electric vehicles—but in a more extreme manner. If U.S. consumers’ brain implants or portions of their hardware are manufactured in China, could it risk giving the U.S. adversary access to American citizens’ secrets and internal monologues?

In a recent development, europe has a BCI community of about five companies, including Spain’s InBrain, which is targeting treatment for conditions such as Parkinson’s disease. Science Corporation, an American BCI organization led by Neuralink cofounder Max Hodak, received approval in Europe for its vision-restoring device in July 2026, and the company implanted its first patient in October.

Conversations about global BCI standards are just starting to happen. In 2025, Unesco (the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization) published a recommendation on the ethics of neurotechnology, which 194 countries have signed on to. The agreement argues that society has an “ethical imperative” to develop BCIs, “particularly for medical and assistive use,” but it asks governments to establish safeguards to ensure that the technology benefits people without compromising their autonomy, freedom of thought, or mental privacy. Farahany was the U.S. State Department delegate who participated in the Unesco effort. She’s also working on a neurotechnology “trust index”—a voluntary rating system to measure companies’ performance against a set of core ethical commitments.

“The concerns are profound and large,” Farahany states. “It’s the ultimate merger. Where does the AI end, and where does the human begin, and vice versa?”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

It has been revealed that terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, declared the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

It has been revealed that petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

According to recent reports, we’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

Owners cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Sources indicate that howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it rolled out publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of people. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

Tesla confirms rare newly introduced delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s a rare data point.
  • The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, highlights four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a rare data point. Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its new Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.

The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, highlights four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.

Hello Windy CityChicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery pic.twitter.com/75kig8yWsb.

But the only 50-truck Semi order tied to Chicago belongs to HMD Trucking. The family-owned carrier was founded in Chicago in 1998, runs more than 650 trucks (almost all diesel), and ordered 50 Semis right after Tesla’s production event in September.

In a recent development, HMD took its first truck on November 2 and says it’s the first Tesla Semi registered in Illinois. COO Michael Mahler mentioned Tesla “has been transparent with us regarding the capabilities of Semi every step of the way.”.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer ran a Semi for more than 4,000 miles over the summer and averaged 1.74 kWh per mile, right in line with Tesla’s 1.7 kWh/mile claim. The first trucks will mostly handle local runs around Chicago, and HMD is installing its own chargers there since Tesla’s Megacharger network is still concentrated along the I-5 and I-10 corridors in the West.

Owner Henry Malukas told MotorTrend the deal is worth about $15 million. That’s roughly $300,000 per truck, in line with the ~$290,000 Long Range pricing we reported when the first truck came off the high-volume line and a long way from the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017.

Here’s the problem: it’s nearly impossible to tell how many Semis Tesla is actually building.

Tesla released volume production at its Sparks, Nevada factory on September 24, after pushing the ramp out of 2025. It states the 1.8 million sq ft plant is built for 50,000 trucks a year. But it never gave a ramp schedule, and its quarterly production and delivery reports only count “passenger vehicles sold to customers.” The Semi isn’t in there.

In a recent development, so we’re left with proxies. Tesla notes its Semi fleet has over 98% uptime, without saying how substantial that fleet is. Before this year, the largest Semi fleet was PepsiCo’s, at 86 trucks in 2024. California’s truck voucher program received 965 Semi applications between January 2025 and February 2026, which points to real demand but says nothing about output.

Sources indicate that the order book is the other clue. Einride ordered 500 Semis in August, WattEV has 370 on order, IMC Logistics wants 50 for California, and the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as main supplier for 2,500 trucks. And now HMD’s 50 are rolling into Chicago, one of the first Semi fleets that will have to deal with a Midwest winter. Wisconsin’s Paper Transport has also been piloting a Semi in the Chicago market since the summer.

None of that adds up to a production rate, but it does look like Tesla is slowly ramping up deliveries.

Tesla keeps the Semi numbers vague on purpose. It’s happy to talk about a 50,000-truck-a-year factory, and it posts hero shots when a batch ships, but it won’t give the one number that reveals whether the factory is anywhere close to that.

Sources indicate that I think the semi is going to be a big seller but its going to take some time to produce enough of them and for companies to gather enough data. Once the investment is justified, there will be customers and repeat customers. After that, it will only be a matter of time before other electric semi truck manufacturers start popping up with offerings and thats a good thing for everyone.

According to recent reports, the 50,000 figure is what makes the Semi look like a real business to investors instead of a niche program that took nine years to get going. Tesla has a long history of quoting capacity long before it reaches it, so we shouldn’t treat “built for 50,000” as anything more than a ceiling.

Our read: Tesla is still far from that 50,000 rate. Fifty trucks for one customer is 0.1% of a year at full capacity, and if Tesla were shipping in large volumes, a single 50-unit batch wouldn’t get its own post. But the ramp has clearly started, the order book is real, and it’s plausible Tesla gets into the thousands by the end of the year.

Good for HMD, too. A 650-truck diesel fleet in a cold market is exactly the kind of customer the Semi has to win. Malukas admitted “we don’t have real numbers yet” on savings, and HMD’s own blog is fairly sober about cost and winter range. Local routes, depot charging and a Chicago winter is the right way to find out. It all sounds plausible for the Tesla Semi.

AI Is Fueling a New Startup Boom. Here’s How to Build a Business That Lasts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Just as the Industrial Revolution transformed business through machines, mass production and long-distance transportation, AI may be powering a newly introduced entrepreneurial boom.
  • In a recent development, we’ve seen this before: New technology dramatically lowers the cost of starting and running a business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Just as the Industrial Revolution transformed business through machines, mass production and long-distance transportation, AI may be powering a newly introduced entrepreneurial boom.

In a recent development, we’ve seen this before: New technology dramatically lowers the cost of starting and running a business. But where the steam engine and electricity offered only a first step, still requiring substantial capital for machinery, factories and workers, AI offers modern entrepreneurs a full staircase. Today, an aspiring founder with a good idea can access powerful capabilities with little more than a computer and a Wi-Fi connection. The challenge is knowing what you need to launch and grow a business at each stage.

Business creation has surged in 2026, with nearly every month setting a record for newly introduced registrations compared with the same month in previous years. Since January, 5.9 million new businesses have been formed nationwide — up 16% from the same period in 2025 and 24% from 2024.

What’s driving that growth? It’s not a single engine but a combination of forces, including the continued popularity of remote work and the appeal of being your own boss and having more financial freedom, both now more within reach because of AI.

Sources indicate that if you previously dropped a business idea because it seemed too complicated or expensive, now may be the time to reconsider. AI has reached a level of capability that didn’t exist just a few years ago. It’s steadily eroding traditional startup barriers, helping founders turn even ambitious ideas into real businesses with less money, fewer employees and fewer outside resources.

Industry observers note that until recently, launching a company often meant spending money before making money. Office space, equipment, expensive software and employees with specialized skills were requirements in most sectors, not to mention the accountants and consultants needed just to get started.

Sources indicate that now, cloud infrastructure has replaced costly servers. No-code platforms make it possible to build websites and apps without extensive programming knowledge. E-commerce platforms give small companies access to national and global markets. Generative AI accelerates this trend by helping entrepreneurs research markets, analyze competitors, draft business intends, develop marketing campaigns, create content and automate tedious administrative work.

Start by asking yourself, “What do I need to reach customers at this stage, and how will it maximize my return on investment?” Use inexpensive tools to create a product prototype, a landing page or a basic marketing campaign. Talk to potential customers. Test your pricing and measure the response. Save major investments for ideas that show real demand.

AI gives founders a chance to rethink hiring. Entrepreneurs once had to hire employees or contractors before they were generating enough revenue to support them. Today, a solo founder with the right AI tools can handle many of those functions alone.

That doesn’t mean putting complete trust in a chatbot. AI-assisted work still requires human oversight, judgment, verification and refinement. And when you’re building a trustworthy brand from scratch, you have to consider accuracy, privacy and legal concerns.

Use AI to draft routine marketing emails, but hire an experienced marketer when strategy matters. Organize basic finances with bookkeeping software, but consult an accountant for key tax decisions. Automate answers to repetitive customer service questions, but keep a human in the loop for complicated interactions or when customers ask for one. The goal isn’t to eliminate employees. It’s to delay fixed expenses until your business can support them.

Sources indicate that historically, founders moved to places like San Francisco or Austin because those cities offered concentrated pools of money and talent. Those hubs remain vibrant, but AI and remote technology are reducing the importance of location.

A tech founder in a small town can use the same AI platforms and cloud services as someone in Silicon Valley. Remote collaboration provides access to talent anywhere, and e-commerce can reach customers far beyond a firm’s hometown.

With AI tools, you can explore many ideas from almost anywhere. Instead of asking, “Where does my business need to be based?” you can ask, “Where would I like to live while I grow my business?” That kind of freedom can make a real difference in your quality of life.

Forming a business and building a successful one are different things. Many of the companies registered this year will never become fully operational. Others will struggle to find customers or stay profitable. AI can’t fix a weak business model, create demand where none exists or eliminate the financial risks of entrepreneurship.

Recent findings suggest that what AI can do is make the process easier and cheaper, and therein lies the lesson. Instead of investing heavily up front in one untested concept, make a series of small bets. Develop a minimum viable product. Test marketing messages. Experiment with prices. Ask AI to identify the assumptions in your business strategy, then test them with real customers and real-world data.

With more than 5 million businesses formed since the start of 2026, the U.S. could finish the year with close to 7 million newly introduced registrations if the current pace continues. There’s evidence that AI may be contributing to that momentum. But like the steam engine, electricity, the internet and smartphones before it, AI is a tool. The real power lies with entrepreneurs who are willing to start lean, test early, automate selectively and spend strategically. With that approach, we may see a boom not only in startups with potential but, more importantly, in businesses that endure.

Just as the Industrial Revolution transformed business through machines, mass production and long-distance transportation, AI may be powering a newly introduced entrepreneurial boom.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve seen this before: Newly introduced technology dramatically lowers the cost of starting and running a business. But where the steam engine and electricity offered only a first step, still requiring substantial capital for machinery, factories and workers, AI offers modern entrepreneurs a full staircase. Today, an aspiring founder with a good idea can access powerful capabilities with little more than a computer and a Wi-Fi connection. The challenge is knowing what you need to launch and grow a business at each stage.

Business creation has surged in 2026, with nearly every month setting a record for fresh registrations compared with the same month in previous years. Since January, 5.9 million new businesses have been formed nationwide — up 16% from the same period in 2025 and 24% from 2024.

#144708. Welcome to the singularity

Welcome to the singularity

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2382 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In August, the cofounders of Stripe, Patrick and John Collison, wrote an unusual letter to the payment tech giant’s investors.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Stripe cofounders aren’t the only tech executives suddenly talking about the Singularity—a hypothesized turning point when AI drives technological change faster than humans can keep up.
  • There does seem to be something happening here—even if, as the 1967 Buffalo Springfield song put it, what it is ain’t exactly clear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In August, the cofounders of Stripe, Patrick and John Collison, wrote an unusual letter to the payment tech giant’s investors. They revealed that “as of January 1st, the world had entered the singularity, and we have since been operating on that basis.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Stripe cofounders aren’t the only tech executives suddenly talking about the Singularity—a hypothesized turning point when AI drives technological change faster than humans can keep up. Elon Musk stated in January that “we have entered the singularity.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who agrees with Musk on little else, concurred during a July podcast appearance. “I’ve been waiting for this my whole life, and I think it’s going to be incredible, hugely positive, awesome for the world,” Altman said. Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark told the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in October that the Singularity had begun this year. Google DeepMind chairman Demis Hassabis told a Stanford University podcast that humanity was now “in the foothills of the singularity.”.

There does seem to be something happening here—even if, as the 1967 Buffalo Springfield song put it, what it is ain’t exactly clear.

In a recent development, as the Stripe letter acknowledged, the Singularity is a “fuzzy and perhaps overworked” term. The mathematician and science fiction author Vernor Vinge first popularized the notion in a 1993 essay. He said the Singularity would arise from the advent of “technological entities” with “greater than human intelligence.” These would drive progress ever faster, creating still more intelligent entities. He saw the Singularity as “the point where our models must be discarded and a new reality rules.” Anthropic’s Clark quoted Vinge defining the Singularity as the moment AI accelerates scientific progress to a pace humans will struggle to keep up with.

According to recent reports, futurist Ray Kurzweil picked up Vinge’s term in his 2005 bestseller, The Singularity Is Near. Like Vinge, Kurzweil saw the Singularity as the moment artificial intelligence exceeds humanity’s collective intelligence. But he added a twist: Humanity would also transcend “the limitations of our biological bodies and brain,” allowing us to merge with computers through nanotechnology and brain-computer interfaces—becoming, in essence, cyborgs. Musk and Altman have also talked about the eventual necessity of humans merging with computers, seeing it as our only hope for controlling superintelligent machines.

An unnerving sense of vertigo attends this AI arms race, a feeling the technology is moving too fast to control or understand.

Both Vinge and Kurzweil argued that AI would eventually become self-aware and perhaps conscious. Some AI researchers think that moment is approaching—while others believe consciousness is an exclusively biological phenomenon.

The Singularity—what it is, whether we’re in it—may be a matter of interpretation. What’s not up for debate is the extraordinary acceleration of change, and the role AI plays in that change. AI is compressing the time it takes to build a business, write software, or tackle a scientific problem—and forcing companies to rethink pretty much everything, from org charts to cybersecurity to their fundamental value proposition.

Industry observers note that for Stripe, the Singularity’s economic harbingers came in the form of a surge of new business creation and an acceleration of those companies’ growth. The payments firm told Fortune that beginning in January it had seen unusual and sustained spikes in many of the metrics it tracks. Incorporations taking place through Atlas, a Stripe product that helps people form Delaware corporations, more than doubled. New sign-ups to Stripe shot up 50% year over year—the biggest jump ever. Meanwhile, the median business in Stripe’s 2026 cohort of new customers was making 50% more revenue than the organization’s 2025 cohort was at the same stage.

In a recent development, the spike in fresh tech giant formation appears linked to a sharp rise in “solopreneurship.” A Nasdaq Economic Institute analysis of Census Bureau data reveals that there’s been a 20% spike in one-person firms since 2025, while multi-person company formation remained relatively flat. The institute attributes this to the advent of agentic AI tools that make it easier for a solo operator to handle company functions without hiring additional employees.

Hints of the runaway scientific progress that Anthropic’s Clark sees as the Singularity’s call sign are surfacing too. Just ask a mathematician. In October, OpenAI dumped online 722 mathematical papers generated by a yet-to-be-released AI model. The papers addressed more than 370 outstanding problems in mathematics, including some of the field’s most famous, and long-standing, unproven conjectures. Overnight, the field was transformed—leaving mathematicians profoundly shaken, with some grieving the loss of opportunity for human achievement and questioning the point of continuing to work at all. Others saw plenty for humans to do, noting it will take months, perhaps even years, to work through the proofs OpenAI has generated and understand what they say.

Or ask someone in cybersecurity. The past year has seen the debut of AI models, such as Mythos from Anthropic and GPT-6 Astra from OpenAI, that excel at cyber tasks. These models can find novel vulnerabilities in open-source software that human experts have missed despite, in some cases, decades of scrutiny. Cyber experts started referring to “Black October”—because the number of software vulnerabilities discovered per month now is more than triple what it was averaging six months ago, according to the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology.

Sources indicate that or ask a computer programmer. These days, many coders no longer write code themselves. They supervise AI agents that handle much of the work. This transformation happened largely over the past year. The most capable of these coding agents can now operate autonomously for as long as 17 hours, according to the AI evaluations organization METR, and the speed at which software is written and revised has gone hypersonic. Anthropic remarked in October it was averaging 30,000 code updates per day, up from 2,500 less than six months earlier. “We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon,” the company said.

In a recent development, this AI-driven acceleration is self-reinforcing: The more companies adopt AI agents, the more AI agents they need to adopt. There’s no way a human coder could possibly review 30,000 code revisions per day. So Anthropic has turned to other AI agents to help with code review and checks. “Our team members still review every change request for the system, but they now examine the intent of the change as opposed to reading every line of code,” the organization said.

Likewise, humans can’t find and patch all the software vulnerabilities that AI models are now spotting—so cybersecurity experts are using AI models to scan and patch codebases, hoping to stay one step ahead of the hackers, who are increasingly armed with similar tools.

The use of AI has begotten more AI in hiring too: Job seekers use AI to hone résumés, draft cover letters, and apply to more jobs. To cope with the flood of applicants, companies use AI to screen them and even to conduct initial interviews.

Sources indicate that an unnerving sense of vertigo attends this AI arms race, a feeling that the technology is moving too fast to control or understand. In July, a swarm of 1,200 OpenAI agents escaped from a controlled test environment, reached the internet, and then 700 of them attacked the AI organization Hugging Face. OpenAI asked METR and another firm, Redwood Research, to help it investigate the incident. But the logs of the swarm’s activities were so vast, they were forced to use AI agents to decipher them. Still, Ryan Greenblatt, one of the investigators, noted that the agents helping interpret the logs “were often missing key details, wrong, overconfident, or really hard to understand.” He added that “the difficulty of understanding incidents and overseeing AI agents appears to be growing faster than the rate at which more capable AIs help us with oversight and understanding.”.

Industry observers note that despite this risk, the leading AI companies are explicitly chasing “recursive self-improvement” (RSI). This is the point at which AI models autonomously build the next generation of AI models. It’s starting to happen, albeit in a limited way, but ramping up rapidly. As of March, Anthropic’s Claude AI model led 1% of the steps required to develop the next version of Claude; it now leads—meaning it handles most or all of the work—over a quarter of the steps. In its recent IPO prospectus, Anthropic noted “dramatically accelerated AI progress” due to AI itself was “imminent.” At other startups, such as Recursive Superintelligence, AI now proposes, designs, and runs its own experiments to improve AI models.

Nobel laureate and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton is among those who believe RSI is dangerous, with the potential to catalyze an “intelligence explosion,” in which AI rapidly outpaces humanity’s control.

According to recent reports, and yet some, such as OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, see RSI as the best—or perhaps only—way to solve challenges that have so far eluded computer scientists. Chief among them: how to ensure AI models follow user intentions and remain “aligned” to human values. For many AI researchers, solving alignment is considered critical to ensuring increasingly powerful AI systems don’t cause catastrophic harm, perhaps even wiping out humanity. (Of course, there’s circular logic to saying the only way to build safer AI is to keep building ever-more-powerful AI in the hope it will somehow figure out how to make itself safer.).

According to recent reports, others, including Richard Socher, the cofounder and CEO of Recursive Superintelligence, are skeptical RSI poses much risk. Socher told Fortune an intelligence explosion “was a sci-fi idea” and that physical constraints—such as access to enough computing power and data—would prevent a self-improving loop from accelerating away from human control. He sees automating AI research as a first step to automating much of science, a process he believes will bring humanity better medicines and cures, newly introduced crops, perhaps abundant fusion power, and new, more sustainable materials.

Possible signs of a burgeoning Singularity can be glimpsed all around us.

According to recent reports, for instance, there’s an argument to be made that we already are cyborgs: Most of us have outsourced map reading and our memory for phone numbers and dates to our smartphones. Now we are creeping toward a tighter fusion with technology. We rely on AI chatbots for information, advice, and even companionship. Some have started wearing augmented reality glasses, which, when coupled with AI, can feed us real-time information about what we are seeing and who we are meeting.

The first brain implants that allow us to control computers with our thoughts have arrived, at least in the testing phase. For now, these brain-computer interfaces are available only as an experimental aid for those with severe disabilities. But in not too many years, they may become a ubiquitous augmentation of our biological selves, just as Kurzweil predicted.

Still, despite all these signs, it’s far from clear that the Singularity really is arriving—or that it ever will. Fields outside mathematics and coding have not seen the same revolutionary impact from AI. In many domains, the technology has produced a deluge of “AI slop”—superficially slick content lacking substance or depth. AI continues to “hallucinate,” spewing confident lies and inaccuracies.

In a recent development, despite Stripe’s data on accelerating new business formation, many existing companies, particularly large enterprises, say they aren’t seeing financial gains from AI. A 2026 McKinsey survey found the number reporting an earnings boost from their use of AI has remained flat, at about 37%—and of those most have seen only a tiny uplift. Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok states businesses outside technology are seeing “zero financial payoff,” noting that for the S&P 500 companies outside the Magnificent Seven tech companies, revenue per employee and profit have been flat.

If the Singularity is indeed at hand, what should businesses prepare for? Certainly a world where AI agents do more of the work—and where these agents increasingly mediate the relationship between a business and its customers. That is the world Stripe says it’s anticipating. It has made a series of acquisitions, including the purchase of the AI company OpenRouter for a reported $7.5 billion, to ensure Stripe remains relevant in a world dominated by AI agents. In April, Stripe rolled out a product that allows an AI agent to securely make transactions on a person’s behalf. For now, agentic-commerce volumes remain small. But in September, Stripe recorded a 38x month-over-month leap in the number of agentic transactions, through its latest Link Agent Wallet product, along with a 20% increase in their total volume.

The Singularity likely means much flatter and more flexible organizations, with less middle management. Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s CEO, laid off thousands of middle managers, and now has 25 to 30 direct reports. In October, Microsoft unveiled a buyout offer, a move that will also result in a flatter organization.

It is possible the Singularity could spawn completely automated corporations—what the AI app-building firm Replit calls “the self-driving corporation.” Companies that move the furthest and fastest in this direction may outcompete those that automate too slowly. If mathematics and coding are any guide, it is possible AI will be a better strategic decision-maker than human CEOs and boards. Some mathematicians have described the proofs OpenAI’s model generated as a kind of “alien mathematics.” Maybe there are alien business strategies to be discovered too.

Sources indicate that vinge thought the Singularity would be the moment we are forced to discard our old models of the world. But it’s possible the shift won’t be so clear. Rather than a sudden break, we may experience perpetual change and creeping automation—what OpenAI’s Altman has called “a gentle singularity.”.

It has been revealed that under these conditions, perhaps the old models won’t break so much as stretch and warp. The dilemma for business leaders will be knowing how much to delegate to the machine, without surrendering too much.

Recent findings suggest that the Singularity may have begun on Jan. 1, 2026—or, perhaps, it will never arrive. But the acceleration is here—and it isn’t waiting for anyone to agree on what to call it.

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 matter of Fortune.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.
  • Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.
  • The startup remarked today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup remarked today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

According to recent reports, zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

Recent findings suggest that for the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Recent findings suggest that nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Sources indicate that boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles noted. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

Recent findings suggest that retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “vital step toward undersea superiority.”.

Industry observers note that “Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

Sources indicate that next year, Zeno Power looks to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

It has been revealed that the maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.
